title: What are some applications of homotopy in topology other than constructing fundamental group (and higher homotopy groups)??
body: In pretty much all books I've seen, homotopy is introduced for the pure purposes of defining the fundamental group. But, what are some other of uses of homotopy? One that I found is that it can be used to characterize path connectedness; Two functions from a given topological space to the space with only a point (and of course, obvious topology) is homotopic, iff all functions between these two spaces are homotopic relative to the empty set. Furthermore, we can check if a space has holes (in a very geometric sense) by checking if a map of circle into a space is homotopic to a constant function relative to a single point on the circle. I am also aware of the application in complex analysis where the complex line integral between two points can be shown to have the same value on paths upto homotopy.

title: Converse of Intermediate Value Theorem via Nonstandard Analysis
body: I am working through Goldblatt's Lectures on the Hyperreals , and I am stuck on Exercise 7.8.4 (p. 82). It is a converse to the Intermediate Value Theorem: "Let the real function $f$ be monotonic on $[a,b]$ , and suppose that for all real $r$ between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ there exists a real $c\in[a,b]$ such that $f(c)=r$ . Prove that $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ ." Standard proofs are abundant. I am specifically looking for a proof using nonstandard analysis. For instance, for continuity I am anticipating that I will have to show that for every $c\in[a,b]$ and for every (hyperreal) $x\in{}^*\mathbb{R}$ such that $x\simeq c$ , we have $f(x)\simeq f(c)$ . The notation $a\simeq b$ means that $a$ is "infinitely close" to $b$ , meaning $a-b$ is infinitesimal. For the most part, Goldblatt exercises are short and sweet, but this one is completely evading me. I've tried many things (both direct and by contradiction) but can't possibly include them all here. I can't seem to formulate a helpful statement to use transfer on. Say I start with $x\simeq c$ . If $x=c$ , then of course $f(x)\simeq f(c)$ . So let's try the case $x>c$ . By transferring monotonicity (assuming, say, nondecreasing), we should have $f(x)\ge f(c)$ . If $f(x)=f(c)$ , we are again done, so let's assume $f(x)>f(c)$ . So at this point we could take an arbitrary $f(x)>y>f(c)$ . By transferring the IVT property, we would get some $x'\in{}^*\mathbb{R}$ such that $c<x'<x$ and $y=f(x')$ . This would imply that $x'\simeq c$ , but I'm not sure what more this says. I could take a sequence of $y$ 's that get closer to $f(c)$ , but I'm not sure how that would imply the original $f(x)$ is infinitely close to $f(c)$ . This is starting to feel like a standard proof anyway.

title: A category has local initial objects if and only if it has a coreflective subgroupoid
body: Given a category $C$ , say that $C$ has local initial objects if every slice category of $C$ has an initial object. In category theory, there are two different meanings of "locally": one applying to Hom-sets, and the other to slice categories. The former applies to "locally small", while the latter applies to "locally cartesian closed". The latter meaning is used above. Then, is it true that a category $C$ has local initial objects if and only if $C$ has a coreflective subcategory that is a groupoid? For the "only if" direction, let $D$ be the full subcategory of objects $X$ of $C$ for which the slice category $C/X$ has a zero object (note that $(X, \mathrm{id}_X)$ is always terminal, so it also needs to be initial for it to be a zero object). Then, for any object $X$ of $C$ , the initial object of $C/X$ should give a coreflection of $X$ in $D$ . Also, every morphism in $D$ should be an isomorphism (making $D$ a subgroupoid of $C$ ). Conversely, for the "if" direction, let $D$ be a coreflective subgroupoid of $C$ . Then, for any object $X$ of $C$ , the coreflection of $X$ in $D$ should give an initial object of $C/X$ . Is the above correct?

title: Formalizing the notion of gluing in topology
body: I am trying to completly formalise the intuitive idea of Gluing in topology. To give some context to this question, let me give an example of constructing the cylinder out of a square. Constructing the cylinder out of quotient Consider the rectangle $[0,1]^2$ , we formalise gluing the left and right edge as quotienting the set by the minimal equivalence relation generated out of the relation $(0,t) \sim (0,1),\forall t \in I $ , then the resulting space $ [0,1]^2/\sim$ is the cylinder. Constructing the cylinder out of the subspace topology Consider the set $S^1 \times [0,1]$ , we give it the subspace topology from $\mathbb{R^3}$ . Discussion As seen in the above, on an intuitive level, it is pretty easy to see that cylinder should be the same whether it is constructed out of a quotient, or constructed out of the interval which itself has the subspace topology. I have a feeling that if we quotient out any set $\mathbb{R^d}$ and give the quotiented set the quotient of the subspace topology, then that be neccesarily homemorphic to some subset $\mathbb{R^n}$ with subspace topology. (A) Now, do note that once we do the quotient of a set which is a subset of a bigger set, the resulting set is a set of equivalence classes, hence that is no longer a subset of the originally said bigger set. I believe that the subset of $\mathbb{R^n}$ that our quotient is homemorphic too should be the one seen as the result of the gluing action (its should be pretty clear that when we the ends of a paper together in 3D space, we get again something that gets again an induced sense of nearness i.e: topology from the ambient space that it exists in). title: Counting f-invariant subspaces over finite fields
body: Riffing off of On the number of $f$ -stable subsets which I very much enjoyed thinking about, let $f : V \to V$ be a linear map on an $n$ -dimensional vector space over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ and define $I(f) = \{ W \subseteq V : f(W) \subseteq W \}$ to be the number of $f$ -invariant subspaces of $W$ . What can we say about the number $I(f)$ ? In addition to considering the question for a fixed value of $f$ , it's also interesting to consider two ways $f$ can vary in families: first, given $f$ defined over $\mathbb{F}_q$ we can extend scalars to define $f/\mathbb{F}_{q^k}$ over $\mathbb{F}_{q^k}$ , and consider the family of counts $I(f/\mathbb{F}_{q^k})$ . Second, given $f$ defined over $\mathbb{Z}$ (so acting on a finite free $\mathbb{Z}$ -module) we can extend scalars to define $f/\mathbb{F}_q$ over any finite field, and consider the family of counts $I(f/\mathbb{F}_q)$ . I think taking $f$ -invariant subspaces defines a scheme, specifically a projective subscheme of the disjoint union of the Grassmannians $\text{Gr}_k(V)$ ; if so these point counts are related to the cohomology of this scheme by the Weil conjectures . Anyway, here's what I've got so far. The easiest special case is that $f$ is diagonalizable over $\mathbb{F}_q$ with distinct eigenvalues; in this case an $f$ -invariant subspace is exactly a direct sum of some subset of the $1$ -dimensional eigenspaces, which gives $I(f) = 2^n$ . This is analogous to the case where $f$ is the identity in the set version of the problem. If $f$ is diagonalizable over $\mathbb{F}_q$ but its eigenspaces have dimensions $m_{\lambda} = \dim V_{\lambda}$ , then an $f$ -invariant subspace is a direct sum of subspaces of the eigenspaces, which gives $$I(f) = \prod_{\lambda} \left( \sum_{k=0}^{m_{\lambda}} {m_{\lambda} \choose k}_q \right)$$ where ${n \choose k}_q$ is the $q$ -binomial coefficients , so the factor in the product corresponding to $\lambda$ counts the total number of subspaces of $V_{\lambda}$ . This is analogous to the case where $f$ is invertible in the set version of the problem. In scheme terms, the scheme of $f$ -invariant subspaces in this case is a product of disjoint unions of Grassmannians. This calculation correctly suggests that we can reduce to considering one (generalized) eigenspace at a time. More precisely, if the characteristic polynomial of $f$ has irreducible factorization $\prod p_i(t)^{m_i}$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ , and we write $V$ as a direct sum of the generalized eigenspaces $V_i = \ker(p_i(f)^{m_i})$ and write $f_i : V_i \to V_i$ for the corresponding restrictions, then an $f$ -invariant subspace of $V$ is exactly a tuple of $f_i$ -invariant subspaces of each $V_i$ , so $$I(f) = \prod_i I(f_i).$$ (This follows e.g. from the Chinese remainder theorem applied to the $\mathbb{F}_q[t]/\prod p_i(t)^{m_i}$ -module structure on $V$ where $t$ acts by $f$ .) So we can reduce WLOG to the case that the characteristic polynomial of $f$ is primary (a power of an irreducible). This is analogous to the reduction to the case that $f$ has one connected component in the set case. However, unlike the set case, it is not true that $f$ is multiplicative under direct sums in general, which complicates things. The case that the characteristic polynomial $p(t)$ is irreducible is not so bad; in this case $\mathbb{F}_q[t]/p(t) \cong \mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ is a field so $f$ -invariant subspaces correspond to $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ -subspaces of a $1$ -dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ , of which there are $2$ . So $I(f) = 2$ in this case. The next interesting case after this is the case that the characteristic polynomial has the form $(t - \lambda)^n$ ; since the $f$ -invariant subspaces don't change if we replace $f$ with $f - \lambda$ we can assume WLOG that $\lambda = 0$ , so we can reduce to the case that $f$ is nilpotent. If $f$ has a single Jordan block then $f$ preserves a complete flag of $V$ given by its generalized eigenspaces $\ker(f^k)$ , and these are the only $f$ -invariant subspaces, so $I(f) = n + 1$ in this case. However the case that $f$ has multiple Jordan blocks seems complicated, and I'm not sure how it works in general. Here Jordan chains are analogous to the "trees" in the set version of the problem. There appears to be a version of the third case of the " $I$ -recursion" (see the original linked question) in this case but I'm not sure how complicated it ends up being. The general case of characteristic polynomial $p(t)^m$ ought to be a mix of the previous two cases but I'm also not sure how it works in general. Also I have not thought much about what happens if $f$ varies in families as described above. Also there is another variant of this question we could ask where we count subgroups of finite abelian groups (this amounts to replacing the polynomial ring $\mathbb{F}_q[t]$ by $\mathbb{Z}$ ), which surely must be known and very classical.

title: Show that the ring of germs at 0 is local
body: I have been posed the following problem: Prove that $C_0$ (which is the ring of germs of continuous functions at $0$ ) is a local ring, with maximal ideal $M$ consisting of the germs of functions that vanish at 0. I have shown that $M$ is maximal in $C_0$ , however to prove locality I have: Let $P$ be an ideal in $C_0$ such that it is not $M$ and there exists a surjective homomorphism $\phi: C_0 \to ℝ$ given by $\phi([f]) = f(0)$ . Then, $P$ is maximal in $C_0$ iff $C_0/P$ is isomorphic to ℝ. We see that ℝ is isomorphic to $C_0/P$ only if $\ker(\phi) = P$ . Since $\ker(\phi)$ is precisely $M$ , $P$ must be $M$ . Therefore, the only maximal ideal in $C_0$ is $M$ and $C_0$ is a local ring. My mentor says my solution is incorrect since I did not use the definition of $C_0$ as a ring of germs , could anyone please clarify what is meant by this?

title: No simple group of order 756 : Burnside's proof
body: I'm interested in a proof of the non-simplicity of groups of order 756. W.R. Scott, Group Theory, p. 392, exerc. 13.4.9, gives it as an easy exercise, but depending on rather advanced results. I have a proof using classical methods (merging theorem, Sylow theorems, Burnside's transfer theorem) and also a theorem of Frobenius of which a particular case says that if $G$ is a finite group, if $d$ is a natural divisor of $|G|$ , then the number of elements $x$ of $G$ such that $x^{d} = 1$ is divisible by $d$ . (There is an English translation of Frobenius's paper by R. Andreev here : https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.08813 ) Unfortunately, my proof is very long. Burnside gave a short proof in 1895 (Collected Papers, vol. I, p. 598-599 of the volume). He assumes that there exists a simple group $G$ of order 756 and here is the beginning of his proof (note that the subgroups of order 27 of $G$ are the Sylow $3$ -subgroups of $G$ ) : "If simple, the group must contain $3^{3}.7$ operations [= elements] of even order and $6.36$ operations of order $7$ , leaving $350$ operations whose orders are powers of $3$ . [Today, we would say : $351$ $3$ -elements.] There are $28$ sub-groups of order $3^{3}$ , and, if any of these have a common sub-group of order $3^{2}$ , the group is certainly composite [= not simple]." So far, no problem. (If anybody is interested, I can explain the details.) But then, Burnside says: "The sub-groups of order 3 which are common to two sub-groups of order $3^{3}$ form a single conjugate set." Since, as noted, the intersection of two different Sylow $3$ -subgroups of $G$ always has order $1$ or $3$ , this amounts to say that the subgroups of order $3$ of $G$ of the form $P \cap Q$ , with $P$ and $Q$ two different Sylow $3$ -subgroups of $G$ , are all conjugate in $G$ . (In any case, I understand it in this manner.) But how can we prove that ? Of course, it would be true if the conjugation action of $G$ on the set of its Sylow $3$ -subgroups was 2-transitive. (And in this case, two different Sylow $3$ -subgroups of $G$ should always have an intersection of order $3$ , since it is easy to prove that if all Sylow 3-subgroups of $G$ intersected pairwise trivially, the group should have more than $756$ elements.) But is it the case that the conjugation action of $G$ on the set of its Sylow $3$ -subgroups is 2-transitive? As a sufficient condition for the conjugation action of a finite group $G$ on the set of its Sylow $p$ -subgroups to be 2-transitive, I only find this (I can give a proof if anybody is interested :) Theorem . Let $G$ be a finite group, let $p$ be a prime divisor of $\vert G \vert$ , let $p^{m}$ denote the greatest power of $p$ dividing $\vert G \vert$ . Assume that 1° $G$ has several Sylow $p$ -subgroups; 2° $a$ is a natural number < $m-1$ such that the intersection of two different Sylow $p$ -subgroups of $G$ is always of order $\leq p^{a}$ ; (we can take $a$ such that $p^{a}$ is the greatest possible order of $P \cap Q$ , with $P$ and $Q$ two different Sylow $p$ -subgroups of $G$ ) 3° for the same $a$ , we have $\vert Syl_{p}(G)\vert < 2 p^{m-a}$ . Then the conjugation action of $G$ on the set of its Sylow $p$ -subgroups is 2-transitive. But, in Burnside's proof, we have $\vert Syl_{3} (G) \vert = 28$ , $m = 3$ and the least possible value we can take for $a$ is $1$ , not $0$ (as already said, it is easy to see that the $3$ -Sylow subgroups of $G$ cannot intersect all pairwise trivially), so condition 3° is not satisfied. Thus my question is : how can we prove Burnside's assertion : "The sub-groups of order 3 which are common to two sub-groups of order $3^{3}$ form a single conjugate set" ? Thanks in advance. $ \mathbf{Edit}$ (July 5, 2024) Thanks to Derek Holt for his clear explanation. I think this explanation enables us to briefly finish the proof. Let $G$ be, by contradiction, a simple group of order $756$ . Let us say that a subroup $R$ of order $3$ of $G$ is multiplist if it is contained in more than one Sylow $3$ -subroup of $G$ and let us say that it is unicist in the other case. Similarly, let us say that an element of order $3$ of $G$ is multiplist if it is contained in more than one Sylow $3$ -subroup of $G$ and let us say that it is unicist in the other case. From Derek Holt's explanation, it results that if $R$ is a multiplist subgroup of order $3$ of $G$ , then $\vert C_{G}(R) \vert = 36$ . Since every proper subgroup of $G$ has order $\leq 36$ , it follows that $\vert N_{G}(R) \vert = 36$ . As stated by Burnside and explained by Derek Holt, all multiplist subgroups of order 3 of $G$ form a conjugacy class, so they are in number $756/36 = 21$ . Thus the multiplist elements of order $3$ of $G$ are in number $42$ . By definition, two distinct Sylow $3$ -subroups of $G$ never have a common unicist element of order $3$ . Moreover, since all Sylow $3$ -subroups of $G$ are conjugate, they all have the same number of unicist elements of order $3$ . Thus (since, as noted by Burnside, $G$ has exactly $28$ Sylow $3$ -subroups) the number of unicist elements of order $3$ in $G$ is divisible by $28 \times \varphi (3)$ and thus by $8$ . As noted by Burnside, two distinct Sylow $3$ -subroups of $G$ never have a common subgroup of order $9$ and thus never have a common element of order $9$ . In the same manner as precedingly, we conclude that the number of elements of order $9$ in $G$ is divisible by $28 \times \varphi (9)$ and thus by $8$ . From the fact that every Sylow $3$ -subroup of $G$ is its own normalizer in $G$ and from Burnside's transfer theorem, we could conclude that the Sylow $3$ -subroups of $G$ are not abelian and thus not cyclic, so $G$ has no element of order $27$ , but without using Burnside's transfer theorem, we can say that clearly no element of order $27$ can be in two distinct Sylow $3$ -subroups of $G$ , so, as above, the number of elements of order $27$ in $G$ is divisible by $28 \times \varphi (27)$ and thus by $8$ . From what precedes, the $3$ -elements of $G$ different from $1$ are in number congruent to $2$ modulo $8$ . But Burnside has shown that the $3$ -elements of $G$ different from $1$ are in number $350$ , not congruent to $2$ modulo $8$ , so we have done. Here is Burnside's complete proof : "If simple, the group must contain $3^{3}.7$ operations [= elements] of even order and $6.36$ operations of order $7$ , leaving $350$ operations whose orders are powers of $3$ . [Today, we would say : $351$ $3$ -elements.] There are $28$ sub-groups of order $3^{3}$ , and, if any of these have a common sub-group of order $3^{2}$ , the group is certainly composite [= not simple]. The sub-groups of order 3 which are common to two sub-groups of order $3^{3}$ form a single conjugate set; and when the group is expressed in $28$ symbols a simple calculation will show that each sub-group of order $3^{3}$ must contain $8$ operations keeping $1$ symbol unchanged and $18$ keeping $4$ symbols unchanged. There are therefore $63$ sub-groups of order $3$ which occur in more than one sub-group of order $3^{3}$ . On the other hand, such a sub-group of order $3$ must (Note VI) be permutable in a sub-group of order $2^{2} /dot 3^{3}$ at least; and must therefore be one of a set of $21$ conjugate sub-groups at most. The supposition that the group is simple thus leads to a contradiction." I don't understand the part of the proof beginning with "and when the group is expressed in $28$ symbols...". Isn't my reasoning sufficient and simpler?

title: A.s. Convergence implies subsequential Complete convergence?
body: The question tries to understand how much stronger is complete convergence as opposed to almost sure convergence. If results that highlight this relationship come to your mind, feel free to share. My question is whether $X_n \xrightarrow{a.s.} X$ implies that for a subsequence $X_{n_K}$ we have that $\sum \mathbb{P}(|X_{n_m} -X|<2^{-m}) < \infty$ , subsequential complete convergence that is (we have here chosen $\varepsilon_m = 2^{-m}$ but any other choice would have been fine as long as $\varepsilon_m \to 0$ ). My reasoning was to use the $\sup$ characterization of a.s. convergence (that is: we have a.s. convergence iff $\mathbb{P}(\sup_n |X_n -X| > 2^{-m}) \to 0$ for all m) to elect an index subsequence $(n_m)$ that satisfies $\mathbb{P}(\sup_n |X_{n_m} -X| > 2^{-m}) < 2^{-m}$ , thus yielding the convergence of the above series. Does that seem reasonable? Do you happen to know more insightful results? Thank you.

title: What is the 2nd most likely value of a Random Walk after time=t?
body: Here is a math problem I was thought of the other day involving Random Walks: Let $X_t$ , $t \in \{0, 1, 2, ..., n\}$ , be a (discrete time) stochastic process where $$X_t \in \{-1, +1\}$$ $$P(X_t = +1) = P(X_t = -1) = 0.5$$ . Let $Z_t$ as the position of $X_t$ at each turn $t$ : $$Z_t = \sum_{i=0}^{t} X_i$$ Using the standard properties of a Random Walk, we know that the position of this process at any given time is Normally Distributed. Using this property, we should be able to find out the mean position and variance after any time $t$ . Here is my question: Suppose at $t=0$ , the process starts at position $0$ .Let's say that we let this process run for $t=15$ steps. In this situation: What is the most likely position this process will be after 15 steps? What is the second most likely position this process will be after 15 steps? What is the third most likely position this process will be after 15 steps? etc. On some level, the answer is somewhat obvious. The distribution of possible positions at time $t$ will begin to resemble a Gaussian Distribution (i.e. Bell Curve) as $t$ increases in size. Therefore, the mean value should be the most frequent - and positions closer to the mean value should relatively more frequent compared to positions farther away from the mean value. However, I would like to try and answer this question more mathematically to determine the exact probability that the process occupies any given position after a certain amount of time. To answer this question, I thought that we can start by enumerating the sample space. After $t$ steps, how many unique values could the process have? I thought about this and naively thought that it can have (- $t$ , $t$ ) number of positions. E.g. if $t$ = 15, then : -15 if 15 consecutive -1 , +15 if 15 consecutive +1 ... and everything else in between. But I am not sure if this logic is correct (e.g. need to account for odd valued $t$ vs even valued $t$ ). However, I am not sure if there is some mathematical function (e.g. combinatorial, probability generator function) which can be used to determine the number of ways a certain position can be reached. If this was possible, then I would be able to find all possible ways to end up with all possible positions, and then rank each one in terms of frequency. Can someone please suggest how to work on this problem? Note: Currently, I am using a computer simulation (in R) to experiment with this problem and enumerate all possible paths and frequencies. For example, here are all the probabilities of all possible paths after 15 turns (I have posted the code in case anyone wants to play with this): library(dplyr) generate_all_paths <- function(num_turns) { if (num_turns == 0) { return(list(c())) } else { paths_plus <- generate_all_paths(num_turns - 1) paths_minus <- generate_all_paths(num_turns - 1) paths_plus <- lapply(paths_plus, c, 1) paths_minus <- lapply(paths_minus, c, -1) return(c(paths_plus, paths_minus)) } } paths <- generate_all_paths(15) df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(paths, function(x) { c(x, rep(NA, max(lengths(paths)) - length(x))) })) df <- as.data.frame(df, stringsAsFactors = FALSE) df$final_score <- rowSums(df, na.rm = TRUE) df <- df %>% group_by(final_score) %>% summarise(count = n()) %>% mutate(probability = count / sum(count)) df Now we can see the frequencies and probabilities of all possible paths for a particular process: final_score count probability 1 -15 1 0.0000305 2 -13 15 0.000458 3 -11 105 0.00320 4 -9 455 0.0139 5 -7 1365 0.0417 6 -5 3003 0.0916 7 -3 5005 0.153 8 -1 6435 0.196 9 1 6435 0.196 10 3 5005 0.153 11 5 3003 0.0916 12 7 1365 0.0417 13 9 455 0.0139 14 11 105 0.00320 15 13 15 0.000458 16 15 1 0.0000305

title: What is this Tensor operation?
body: I am trying to identify an operation that takes two matrices of dimensions $n^2$ and output a matrix of dimensions $n^2$ . Every element in the output matrix incorporates all elements from the input matrices. All possible multiplication pairs from elements of the input matrices appear only once throughout the output matrix. So individual output elements have all distinct pairs. Here is an example given the matrices: $$ A = \left[\begin{array}{cc} a_{11} &a_{12} \\ a_{21} &a_{22} \end{array}\right] \;\; , \;\; B = \left[\begin{array}{cc} b_{11} &b_{12} \\ b_{21} &b_{22} \end{array}\right]$$ What is the operation that produce: $$operation(A,B) = \left[\begin{array} \\ a_{11}b_{11}+a_{12}b_{21}+a_{22}b_{12}+a_{21}b_{22} & a_{11}b_{12}+a_{12}b_{22}+a_{22}b_{11}+a_{21}b_{21} \\ a_{21}b_{11}+a_{22}b_{21}+a_{12}b_{12}+a_{11}b_{22} & a_{21}b_{12}+a_{22}b_{22}+a_{12}b_{11}+a_{11}b_{21} \end{array}\right]$$ I find out that it is equivalent to these matrix multiplications; $$operation(A,B) = AB + C_{up} A C_{up} C_{left} B$$ Where $C_{up}$ is a up Cyclic permutation and $C_{left}$ a left one. The second term is basically the following matrix multiplication: $$\left[\begin{matrix} a_{21} & a_{22} \\ a_{11} & a_{12} \end{matrix}\right]\left[\begin{matrix} b_{22} & b_{21} \\ b_{12} & b_{11} \end{matrix}\right]$$ If the matrices are 3x3 instead of 2x2, the result become: $$operation(A,B) = AB + C_{up}A C_{up} C_{left} B + C_{down} A C_{down} C_{right} B$$ Does it relate to a standard tensor operation?

title: Using the theory of simplicial complex to construct a deformation retraction
body: Let $X$ be a complex manifold and $Y$ the normal complex analytic space. Let $f: X \to Y$ be a proper surjective holomorphic map with connected fibers. In a paper, the author told us that, for any point $y\in Y$ , by the Lojaziewic's triangulation theorem, we can choose an open Stein neighborhood $U$ such that there is a deformation retraction $f^{-1}(U)\to X_y:=f^{-1}(y)$ . Question: Why can we choose such $U$ (or how to choose such $U$ )? Clues: 1, The triangulation theorem appears to be as follows: let $X$ be a complex space and $A$ an analytic subset of $X$ . Then there exists a triangulation of $|X|$ in which $A$ appears as the support of a sub-complex. In particular, there exists an open neighbourhood $E$ of $A$ such that $E$ and $\bar{E}$ can be retracted onto $A$ . 2, Consequently, our above question may be reduced to be a purely algebraically-topologically question: how to use the theory of simplicial complex to find such $U$ satisfying that there is a deformation retraction $f^{-1}(U)\to X_y$ ? P.S. Note that when $Y$ is the unit disk in $\mathbb{C}$ , In page 101 of the book: 1984, Barth, Peters, Van de Ven, Compact Complex Surfaces, the authors told us that there is a deformation retraction $X\to X_0$ ( However, the method there does not seem to be applicable here .). For more details, see the post Using morse theory to construct a deformation retraction

title: Are these Cayley graphs strongly connected?
body: My Background: I have no formal training in graph theory. I'm just a group theory PhD student. He mentioned something about my research from a graph theoretical perspective. It seemed like a known thing, so I will ask about it here. The Question: Is the (directed) Cayley graph $\operatorname{Cay}(G,T)$ of $G=\operatorname{SL}(n,q)$ with respect to $T$ strongly connected, where $$T=\{g^{-1}sg, g^{-1}s^{-1}g\mid s\in S, g\in G\}$$ for arbitrary, normally generating $S\subseteq G$ , i.e. , $G=\operatorname{ncl}_G(S)$ ? The Details: A graph is strongly connected if for any vertices $x,y$ , there exists a path from $x$ to $y$ and vice versa. Context: Since . . . This is probably known already. I have very little experience with graph theory. It would greatly inform my research. I am unlikely to be able to prove it myself. . . . I would massively appreciate a proof (or counterexample) aimed at an advanced undergraduate level. Thoughts: I think it might have something to do with $T$ being closed under inverses.

title: Kahler differentials and etale fundamental group
body: In Algebraic geometry we can define two notions that generalize tools from topology/differential geometry: the etale fundamental group and the module/sheaf of Kähler differentials. In the complex setting (ie when dealing with an affine or projective smooth complex manifold $X$ ), we can assume both points of view and we can also introduce the integral of a 1-form, say $\omega$ , along a loop $\gamma$ . If $\omega$ is closed we have homotopy invariance of the integral and, thanks to Stokes theorem, we can define a map $\int:\pi_1(X,x)×H^1_{dR}(X,\mathbb{C})\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ with nice properties. Of course, to be precise, integration is not defined over non-smooth submanifolds in general, but we can take the homology class of $\gamma$ , and it is a well known fact that in that setting the construction works. So here's the question: does this construction of a pairing in any way generalizes when we consider $X$ as a scheme, replacing the fundamental group with its étale counterpart and holomorphic differentials with algebraic ones? And if that is possible does this works even for more general schemes?

My attempt on the problem is like so: If the median is $60$ , then the sum of the $180$ th and the $181$ st should be $120$ - so that the average between them (since we have an even number of students) is $60$ . Let $i$ denote the grade student $180$ got, $20\leq i\leq 60$ (lower than 20 would cause the $181st$ have grade above $100$ , and higher than $60$ would cause $181$ st have grade below $180$ th. So the $181$ th has grade $120 - i$ . Now let's count the historgrams for the $179$ students who got less than or equal to $i$ (between $0-i$ inclusive): it's a choice with repetitions and without regard to the order at which we choose, so according to the stars and bars result: $${179 + i + 1 - 1\choose 179}={179 + i\choose 179}$$ And let's to the same thing for student who go between $120-i$ and $100$ inclusive: $${179 + (100 - (120 - i) + 1) - 1\choose 179}={159 + i\choose 179}$$ Multiplying both results since they come one after the other and summing it all up, we end up with: $$\sum_{i=20}^{60}{179 + i\choose 179}{159 + i\choose 179}$$ Now, as I asked at the beggining of the question, I would like to know if there is a solution not using sums, but a closed a formula. title: Improving Ellipsoid Theorem $t+\mathcal{E} \subseteq K \subset t + c\cdot n \mathcal{E}$
body: Setting: Definition (ellipsoid): An ellipsoid is $\mathcal{E} := \{y \in \mathbb{R}^n : ||A^{-1}(y-t)|| \leq 1\}$ , i.e images under a given $A$ of full rank of the unit closed ball of $\mathbb{R}^n$ . Definition (convex body): A convex body is a convex compact, with nonempty interior part subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ . Definition (centrally symmetric): $K$ is centrally symmetric if when $x \in K$ then $-x \in K$ I have a proof of the following Theorem: Theorem: For all convex body $K \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ exists $\mathcal{E}$ centered in $0$ and $t \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that $t+\mathcal{E} \subseteq K \subset t + c\cdot n \mathcal{E}$ . where $c$ is a constant independent from $n$ , $c > 130$ . Goal: What I'd like to construct is a proof for Theorem: For all centrally symmetric convex body $K \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ exists $\mathcal{E}$ centered in $0$ and $t \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that $t+\mathcal{E} \subseteq K \subset t + c\cdot \sqrt{n} \mathcal{E}$ . Outline of the proof: I want to modify the proof of the previous theorem, essentially the idea of the proof is to argue by contradiction, wlog using the unit ball. So we find a point $z \in K$ with norm $cn$ by convexity of $K$ , which, up to rotation can be brought onto the $e_1$ direction. Now the idea is to look at the convex hull of $B(0,1) \cup \{cn e_1\}$ and argument to find an ellipsoid inside $K$ with volume greater of the unit ball $V_n$ , ending the proof. The proof is constructive i.e $$\mathcal{E'} := x \in \mathbb{R}^n : \sum\limits_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\alpha^2_i}(x_i-t_i)^2 \leq 1$$ , where $t = e_1, \alpha_1 = 2,\alpha_i = \sqrt{\frac{n}{n+(1/10)}}$ for $i\geq 2$ . In particular $vol(\mathcal{E'}) > V_n$ if and only if $2\cdot(\frac{n}{n+\frac{1}{10}})^{\frac{n-1}{2}} > 1$ which is (incredibly) true because of $$ 2\cdot(\frac{n}{n+\frac{1}{10}})^{\frac{n-1}{2}} \geq 2\cdot(\frac{1}{e^{\frac{1}{10n}}})^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\geq 2\cdot(\frac{1}{e^{\frac{1}{10n}}}) \geq 2\cdot(\frac{1}{e^{\frac{1}{20}}}) > 1$$ This is important since if we show that $\mathcal{E'} \subset$ convex hull of $B(0,1) \cup \{cn e_1\}$ we are done. In order to do this, we parametrize the line segment between $cn \cdot e_1$ and a vector $y$ such that $||y|| = 1$ with $y_1 = 0$ , up to rotations we can take $e_2$ and show that for the points of the line segment $x_{\lambda} = \lambda e_2 + (1-\lambda)cn e_1$ it holds that $$\sum\limits_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\alpha^2_i}(x_{\lambda}-t)_i^2 > 1$$ for $\lambda \in [0,1]$ . This is true because if $\lambda \geq 1 - \frac{1}{30n}$ then $(1+\frac{1}{10n})(1-\frac{1}{30n})^2 > 1$ . While for $0 \leq \lambda < 1 - \frac{1}{30n}$ then $\frac{1}{4}((1-\lambda)cn - 1)^2 \geq \frac{1}{4}(\frac{1}{30n}cn-1)^2 > 1$ for $c$ large enough $\Box$ . At this point, I thought take replacing $\alpha_i$ by putting simply $\sqrt{n}$ would have worked (hear the "ice cream" convex hull has two cones so that we can replace t=0, centering it in the origin), and indeed it does with different inequalities and constants if it wasn't that in showing $vol(\mathcal{E'}) > V_n$ I made a mistake not realizing that the basis of the exponential is smaller than $1$ . I know this theorem holds with $C =1$ , for example, a reference can be found in "A course in Convexity" by Barvinok , but I think the proof is unnecessarily complicated since here we don't require that $C=1$ . Do you have an idea how to adjust the argument? Any help would be appreciated.

title: Truncated Tarski's theorem without axiom of choice
body: I read there that the fact about equivalence of $A$ and $A^2$ for any infinite set $A$ and the axiom of choice are equivalent. But what if we prove it only for sets that have cardinality of $\aleph_n, n \in \mathbb{N}\cup\lbrace 0 \rbrace$ . Let's prove it with mathematical induction. For $n = 0$ it's evident, we can use the same proof that was used for the countability of $\mathbb{Q}$ . Suppose that it's true for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ . Let's prove it for $n + 1$ . Consider a set $A$ with cardinality of $\aleph_{n + 1}$ . Then there exists a set $B$ with cardinality of $\aleph_n$ which powerset is equivalent to $A$ : $A \sim 2^B$ . Then every element of $A$ corresponds to a subset of $B$ . We can construct an injection between $(2^B)^2$ and $2^B$ . First, we construct an injection between $(2^B)^2$ and $2^{B^2}$ : $f(S_1, S_2) = S_1 \times S_2$ . Further we can construct an injection between $2^{B^2}$ and $2^B$ by using, as we assume, existing injection between $B^2$ and $B$ . Also we can easily can construct an injection between $2^B$ and $(2^B)^2$ : $f(S) = (S, S)$ . Then by the Cantor-Bernstein theorem we have that $A \sim 2^B \sim (2^B)^2 \sim A^2$ As far as I'm concerned, that proof doesn't use the axiom of choice. But it doesn't work for such cardinals as $\aleph_\omega, \aleph_{\omega + 1}$ and so on, because there we should use transfinite induction which uses the axiom of choice. Did I get it right?

title: Images of structure preserving maps are structures?
body: Context : I have been working with (mostly concrete) categories like Sets, Groups, Rings, Vect $_k$ , Ab, $R$ -Mod, Top, Diff and so on. As I understand it, images of group maps are subgroups of their co-domain groups. Hence images of group maps are groups. Same for other “algebraic categories” in my list. However, this seems to break down for Top and Diff (the category of smooth manifolds and smooth maps between them). In Top I need to specify a topology on the image of the continuous map and it somehow “does not come automatically with a topology” unlike group images which come with a group structure ie the the group structure inherited from the co-domain group. In fact one can show that if the underlying set of the image of a group map has a group structure, then it is indeed this subgroup structure inherited from the co-domain group. Moreover, in Top it may seem somewhat canonical to equip the image with the subspace topology of the co-domain space. At least, it is the coarsest topology that makes the inclusion of the image of a continuous map into its image continuous. However, unlike in Groups, this is not the only structure on the image that makes the inclusion continuous. I feel like, things get even worse in Diff , where it seems to be the case that except when the smooth maps are also smooth embeddings or injective smooth immersions, there is no canonical choice of topology and smooth structure for the image of a smooth map. For instance the figure “8” curve is not even a manifold wrt subspace topology even though it is the image of a smooth map (its not smoothly embedded but it is smoothly immersed in the plane. Question : Why is this happening? More precisely, why is it that in categories of groups and rings, images of structure preserving maps are sets with those structures, but NOT in Top or Diff ? Is there a category theory explanation for this? One possible argument I could expect is that smooth structure and indeed topology are structures that we need add on to sets. But I would really like to see some elaboration on this, if possible.

title: Help with the proof of this statement
body: Let $ f : [a, b] \rightarrow \mathbb{R} $ be a bounded function. Then for every $\epsilon > 0$ , there exists $\delta > 0$ such that for any partition $D$ of the interval $[a, b]$ with norm $\nu(D)$ smaller than $\delta$ , the following holds: $$ \left| U(f, D) - \int_a^b \overline{f}(x) \, dx \right| < \epsilon. $$ The upper Riemann integral is the infimum over all partitions of the upper sum. The left side is an upper sum with respect to partition $D$ . The infimum on all the sums is given by: $\inf_{D} U(f, D)$ The right side is the upper integral, which is the infimum over all partitions of the upper sum: $\overline{\int_a^b} f(x) \, dx = \inf_{D} U(f, D)$ The way I would do it is to get an arbitrary upper sum within $\epsilon/2$ of the integral.

title: If every sequence of Riemann sums of a function converges, is the function integrable?

Let $P_n^\ast$ be the set of sample points from each subinterval of $P_n$ , and $S(f,P_n,P_n^\ast)$ the Riemann sum of $f$ constructed using $P_n$ and $P_n^\ast$ . In Stewart's calculus book, the (Riemann) integrability of $f$ is defined as follows: There exists a real number $L$ such that, for any $\epsilon>0$ , there exists $N\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that if $n\geq N$ , then $$\left|S(f,P_n,P_n^\ast)-L\right|<\epsilon$$ for any choice of $P_n^\ast$ . Note that this condition is stronger than the following condition: There exists a real number $L$ such that the sequence $\{S(f,P_n,P_n^\ast)\}$ of Riemann sums converges to $L$ for any choice of the sequence $\{P_n^\ast\}$ . Presumably the latter condition is not sufficient to guarantee the (Riemann) integrability of $f$ . Does anyone know an example of a non-integrable function satisfying the latter condition?

title: How to deal with ill conditioned optimization problem (Sinkhorn barycenter)
body: Problematic (Debiased Sinkhorn barycenter, proposed by H.Janti et al.): Let $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_K \in \Delta_n$ and $\mathbf{K}=e^{-\frac{\mathrm{C}}{\varepsilon}}$ . Let $\pi$ denote a sequence $\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_K$ of transport plans in $\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n \times n}$ and the constraint sets $\mathcal{H}_1=\left\{\pi \mid \forall k, \pi_k \mathbb{1}=\alpha_k\right\}$ , and $\mathcal{H}_2=\left\{\pi \mid \forall k \forall k^{\prime}, \pi_k^{\top} \mathbb{1}=\pi_{k^{\prime}} \mathbb{1}\right\}$ . The barycenter problem $\min _{\alpha \in \Delta_n} \sum_{k=1}^K w_k \mathrm{~S}_{\varepsilon}\left(\alpha_k, \alpha\right)$ is equivalent to: \begin{align*} & \min _{\substack{\pi \in \mathcal{H}_1 \cap \mathcal{H}_2 \\ d \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^n}}\left[\varepsilon \sum_{k=1}^K w_k \mathrm{KL}\left(\pi_k \mid \mathbf{K} \operatorname{diag}(d)\right) +\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\langle d-\mathbb{1}, \mathbf{K}(d-\mathbb{1})\rangle\right]. \tag{3.} \end{align*} where $\mathrm{KL}(\mathbf{P} \mid \mathbf{Q})=\sum_{i, j} \mathbf{P}_{i j} \log \left(\frac{\mathbf{P}_{i j}}{\mathbf{Q}_{i j}}\right)+\mathbf{Q}_{i j}-\mathbf{P}_{i j}$ . To compute the barycenter numerically, we can use Algorithm 1 in the same paper of Janati . Comments: Algorithm 1 solves the problem quite efficiently with many examples although there is no proof of convergence. However, I found an issue that when the matrix $\mathbf{K}$ has a large condition number, this algorithm is not stable anymore and I have to change the value of $\varepsilon$ to be suitable (but this is not a general way). So, I am trying to reduce the effect of the matrix $\mathbf{K}$ by setting $v = K^{1/2}(d - \mathbb{1})$ and optimize the objective function over this new variable $v$ . I wonder if you could give me some idea to implement or improve this algorithm better.

title: Universal property definition of an ideal generated by a subset?
body: I'm puzzled by the definition of ideals generated by a subset of a ring in Aluffi, Algebra: Ch 0 . The previous chapter on groups is (for an algebra book of this level) quite categorical in spirit. In particular, it gives definitions and proofs in terms of universal properties whenever possible. For example, given a subset $A$ of a group $G$ , the subgroup generated by $A$ is defined as the image of the unique group homomorphism $F(A) \to G$ where $F(A)$ is the free group on $A$ . This perspective returns when the submodule generated by a subset of a module is defined using the universal property of free modules. Meanwhile, however, the definition of the ideal generated by a subset of a ring is more traditional. It is essentially defined to be the smallest ideal of the ring containing the subset. Since the book makes so much effort to give element-free definitions in terms of universal properties, I'm wondering whether such an approach is possible for defining ideals generated by subsets, and if so, why Aluffi is avoiding it. I suppose one cannot hope to straightforwardly mimic the group or module case as the images of ring homomorphisms are not in general ideals.

If $P$ is a prime of $R$ and if $S:=R/P$ contains an element $b \neq 0$ such that $S[b^{-1}]$ is a field then $S$ is a field. Proof. b $\Rightarrow$ a : Let $Q$ be a prime ideal of $R$ , and let $I$ be the intersection of all the maximal ideals containing $Q$ . We must show that $I =Q$ . If, on the contrary, $I\neq Q$ , choose an element $f\in I-Q$ . Nevertheless, $P$ generates a maximal ideal of $R[f^{-1}]$ , so $(R/P)[f^{-1}]$ is a field ( Localization commutes with quotient ) . This contradicts bypothesis b, so $I=Q$ as required. QED. The first order derivatives are relatively easy to obtained, however I'm having trouble establishing the identities of the second order derivatives. In order to solve this, we treat z as an implicit function of x and y, and then solve the function $$G(x,y) = (\frac{dz}{dx}, \frac{dz}{dy})$$ for the point $(x_0, y_0)$ $$G(x_0, y_0) = (\frac{u}{w}, \frac{v}{w})$$ using newton's method. Getting the gradients of the underlying variables x, and z with respect to u, and v is relatively simple (falls directly out of using newton's method), solving the system: $$Jac(G) \begin{bmatrix} dx \\\ dy \\ \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{d^2z}{dx^2} & \frac{d^2z}{dxdy} \\\ \frac{d^2z}{dxdy} & \frac{d^2z}{dy^2} \\ \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{w}\begin{bmatrix} du \\\ dv \\ \end{bmatrix}$$ which we can recognize as an application of the inverse function theorem, thus making the first derivatives the entries of the inverse jacobian: $$\begin{bmatrix} \frac{dx}{du} & \frac{dy}{du} \\\ \frac{dx}{dv} & \frac{dy}{dv} \\ \end{bmatrix} = Jac(G)^{-1} = \frac{1}{det(Jac(G))} \begin{bmatrix} \frac{d^2z}{dy^2} & -\frac{d^2z}{dxdy} \\\ -\frac{d^2z}{dxdy} & \frac{d^2z}{dx^2} \\ \end{bmatrix}$$ We can further solve for the derivatives of x and y with respect to w: $$Jac(G) \begin{bmatrix} dx \\\ dy \\ \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{u}{w^2}dw \\\ \frac{v}{w^2}dw \\ \end{bmatrix}$$ $$\begin{bmatrix} \frac{dx}{dw} \\\ \frac{dy}{dw} \\ \end{bmatrix} = Jac(G)^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} \frac{u}{w^2} \\\ \frac{v}{w^2} \\ \end{bmatrix}$$ and finally the inverse z derivatives: $$\frac{dz}{du} = \frac{dx}{du}\frac{dz}{dx} + \frac{dy}{du}\frac{dz}{dy} = \frac{dx}{du}\frac{u}{w} + \frac{dy}{du}\frac{v}{w}$$ $$\frac{dz}{dv} = \frac{dx}{dv}\frac{dz}{dx} + \frac{dy}{dv}\frac{dz}{dy} = \frac{dx}{dw}\frac{u}{w} + \frac{dy}{dw}\frac{v}{w}$$ $$\frac{dz}{dw} = \frac{dx}{dw}\frac{dz}{dx} + \frac{dy}{dw}\frac{dz}{dy} = \frac{dx}{dw}\frac{u}{w} + \frac{dy}{dw}\frac{v}{w}$$ I have verified all of these derivatives against an various function with finite difference tests, and found them to be correct. I've attempted a number of methods to get the second derivatives of the inverse, however have yet to find one that matches with my calculate finite difference test cases. What is the correct derivation of these? This seems like a problem that should have been studied / have the solution published in a textbook or paper, however I've had trouble finding any.

title: A question about general equations of Hyperbolas
body: We know that the general equation for a hyperbola is $$\sqrt{(x-\alpha)^2+(y-\beta)^2}=e\cdot\frac{|lx+my+n|}{\sqrt{l^2+m^2}}$$ where $(\alpha, \beta)$ is the focus of the hyperbola, $e>1$ is the eccentricity and $lx+my+n=0$ is the directrix. For future answer purposes, I will write the expanded form of this equation below, as it may prove to be helpful: $$x^2(m^2-l^2(e^2-1))+y^2(l^2-m^2(e^2-1))-2lme^2xy-x(2\alpha(l^2+m^2)+2lne^2)-y(2\beta(l^2+m^2)+2mne^2)+(l^2+m^2)(\alpha^2+\beta^2)-n^2e^2=0$$ However, there is also an alternate, much simpler representation of hyperbolas, namely $$L_1L_2=\pm s^2$$ where $L_1$ and $L_2$ are any two intersecting lines where they are represented as $L_{1,2}: ax+by+c=0$ or equivalently $L_{1,2}: y-m_{1,2}x-c_{1,2}=0$ , and $s$ is any positive real number. Specifically, $L_1$ and $L_2$ represent the asymptotes of the given hyperbola, and choosing either the $+$ or $-$ signs give us conjugate hyerbolas for the same set of asymptotes. Amazingly, this also gives us the property that adding the equations of two conjugate hyperbolas (with the same coefficients for $x^2$ and $y^2$ ) give us the combined equation of the asymptotes that describe them. I have a few questions about this representation: 1. Why does this representation represent a hyperbola? I have prepared a GeoGebra document to illustrate this: https://www.geogebra.org/calculator/tc6ghx8f I think I have almost answered this question. We consider the distances of the given point $(x, y)$ from each of the lines $L_1$ and $L_2$ . Say we call these distances $d_1$ and $d_2$ . Then what that form basically says is that the product $d_1d_2=s^2$ (this $s$ is different than the original s) i.e. this product of distances is a constant. I suppose this can be treated as a defining property of hyperbolas, which would confirm the validity of this form. It also explains why choosing opposite signs gives us conjugate hyperbolas, since the "opposite quadrants" defined by the two asymptotes have the same sign of the function $L_1L_2(x,y)=(y-m_1x-c_1)(y-m_2x-c_2)$ so the adjacent quadrants have opposite signs. 2. Does every combination of two non-parallel lines $L_1$ and $L_2$ and the parameter $s$ give us a unique hyperbola? Discounting for mere scalings of the coefficients of the two lines and $s$ , intuitively I believe this must be true. Every pair of intersecting lines, however they are oriented, can have hyperbolas sandwiched in between them, and the parameter $s$ can be thought of as a "distance" parameter, where the smaller $s$ is, the closer the vertices of the hyperbola get to the intersection point of the two lines. And indeed, if we let $s\to 0$ we see that the limiting case of a hyperbola is just its asymptotes. 3. Does this form represent every possible hyperbola? Again, intuitively this seems to be true. Every hyperbola must have a set of asymptotes, and it must also have some associated value of $s$ and an associated sign out of the $\pm$ . However, I don't see how I can justify this. 4. How does this form convert to the focus-directrix form? In other words, how can we find the focus, directrix and eccentricity for any general hyperbola $L_1L_2=\pm s^2$ ? I think this can be solved with the help of linear transformations. shifting the origin as well as scaling and rotating appropriately. However, I wasn't able to make any progress on this at all. Any answers to any of my questions is appreciated! I'm just looking for some clarity on this topic, mainly about how do we rigidly prove all of the facts I presented.

title: Proof by contradiction, where is the contradiction?
body: Example. Let $F=\{E_1,E_2,\ldots,E_s\}$ be a family of subsets with $r$ elements of some set $X$ . Show that if the intersection of any $r+1$ (not necessarily distinct) sets in $F$ is nonempty, then the intersection of all sets in $F$ is nonempty. Solution. Again we assume the contrary, namely that the intersection of all sets in $F$ is empty. Consider the set $E_1=\{x_1,\ldots,x_r\}$ . Because none of the $x_i$ , $i=1,2,\ldots,r$ , lies in the intersection of all the $E_j$ 's (this intersection being empty), it follows that for each $i$ we can find some $E_{j_i}$ such that $x_i\notin E_{j_i}$ . Then $$E_1\cap E_{i_1}\cap E_{i_2}\cap\cdots\cap E_{i_r}=\emptyset,$$ since, at the same time, this intersection is included in $E_1$ and does not contain any element of $E_1$ . But this contradicts the hypothesis. It follows that our initial assumption was false, and hence the sets from the family $F$ have a nonempty intersection. I understand why the intersection of $E_1,E_{i_1},E_{i_2} \ldots$ is empty, but how does this fact contradict the hypothesis? More importantly, what exactly is the hypothesis?

title: Parallel vector field along a geodesic is a Jacobi field?
body: Let $M$ be a manifold with a linear connection $\nabla.$ A vector field $V$ along a curve $\gamma$ is said to be parallel along $\gamma$ with respect to $\nabla$ if $D_tV =0$ . Let $\gamma : I \to M$ be a geodesic and $t_0 \in I$ . Fix a vector $V_0 \in T_{\gamma(t_0)}M$ such that $V_0$ is orthogonal to $\dot{\gamma}(t_0)$ . Then by the Parallel Translation ( John Lee's Introduction to Riemannian manifolds, Theorem 4.32. ), there exists a unique parallel vector field $V$ along $\gamma$ such that $V(t_0) =V_0$ . Note next theorem ( John Lee's book Theorem 10.1 ) : Theorem 10.1. ( The Jacobi Equation ). Let $\gamma$ be a geodesic and $V$ a vector field along $\gamma$ . If $V$ is the variation field of a variation through geodesics, then $V$ satisfies the following equation, called the Jacobi equation : $$ D_t^2V + R(V, \dot{\gamma})\dot{\gamma} = 0. \tag{10.2}$$ A smooth vector feild along a geodesic that satisfies the Jacobi equation is called a Jacobi field. Here, 'variation through geodesics' is defined as follows : Suppose that $I, K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ are intervals, $\gamma : I \to M$ is a geodesic, and $\Gamma : K \times I \to M$ is a variation of $\gamma$ ( as defined in the John Lee's book Chapter 6 ). We say that $\Gamma$ is a variation through geodesics if each of the main curves $\Gamma_s(t)=\Gamma(s,t)$ is also geodesic. Q. Then my question is, the above parallel vector field $V$ is a jacobi field? It suffices to show that $V$ is the variation field of a variation through geodesics. I found next Lemma in the John Lee's book : Lemma 6.1. If $\gamma$ is an admissible curve and $V$ is a piecewise smooth vector field along $\gamma$ , then $V$ is the variation field of some variation of $\gamma$ . If $V$ is proper, the variation cna be taken to be proper as well. This lemma only gaurantees that the above $V$ is the variation field of some variation of $\gamma$ , not the variation field of 'a variation through geodesics'. For the case that $V$ is a 'parallel' vector field along $\gamma$ , such condition is satisfied? This question originates from Existence of a parallel orthonormal frame $(E_1, \dots , E_n)$ along $\gamma$ such that $E_n = \dot{\gamma}$ . In the question I answered myself and not convince that each $E_1, E_2 ,\dots, E_{n-1}$ are normal along $\gamma$ ( In my argument of the answer in my linked question, for $E_1, E_2, \dots, E_{n-1}$ to become normal, they need to be Jacobi fields. ) EDIT : Uhm.. I think that our above question is not true in general. For the original linked question below, I think that $E_1 , \dots E_{n-1}$ are normal along $\gamma$ since $(E_1, \dots , E_{n-1} , E_n = \dot{\gamma} )$ forms an orthonormal frame. title: Dividing $N$ coins into at most $K$ groups such that I can get any number of coins by selecting whole groups
body: Problem Inspired from Dividing $100$ coins into $7$ groups such that I can choose any number of coins by selecting whole groups . I am interested in the number of possible ways we can get such a split. The formal problem statement is: Count the number of multisets $S$ containing positive integers, and of size at most $K$ , where for all $x \in \mathbb{N}, x\le N$ , we can get a subset $A \subseteq S$ such that $\sum_{s\in A} s = x$ . Example: for $N=10, K=5$ , we can get $8$ such multisets: [3, 2, 2, 2, 1] [3, 3, 2, 1, 1] [4, 2, 2, 1, 1] [4, 3, 1, 1, 1] [4, 3, 2, 1] [5, 2, 1, 1, 1] [5, 2, 2, 1] [5, 3, 1, 1] What I've achieved For any such multiset $S$ , let's label the largest integer as $s_0$ . Then we can deduce three things: $s_0 \le \left\lceil \frac{N}{2} \right\rceil$ Proved by contradiction: If $s_0 > \left\lceil \frac{N}{2} \right\rceil$ , then we cannot get any subset $A \subseteq S$ which contains exactly $\left\lceil \frac{N}{2} \right\rceil$ coins. $S \setminus \{s_0\}$ should necessarily hold the same property for $N-s_0$ coins and $K-1$ groups, i.e., for all $x \in \mathbb{N}, x\le N-s_0$ , we can get a subset $A\in S \setminus \{s_0\}$ such that $\sum_{s\in A} s = x$ Proved by contradiction: take the smallest $x_0$ which doesn't hold this property for $S \setminus \{s_0\}$ . Note that $x_0 < s_0$ , because if $x_0 \ge s_0$ , then there must exist an element $s_1 > x_0 \ge s_0$ inside $S \setminus \{s_0\}$ , failing the assumption that $s_0$ is largest. Then as we now know $x_0 < s_0$ , we deduce $x_0$ doesn't satisfy the property for $S$ with $N$ coins too, as any subset $A \subseteq S$ which contains $s_0$ will have a sum $\ge s_0> x_0$ . The above two points are sufficient to show that $S$ satisfies the property too. By construction By the above three properties, we can create a recursion for the number of multisets. Let the number of multisets where all integers $\le s_0$ be defined as $f(N, K, s_0)$ , then $$f(N, K, s_0) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{ if } N=0 \land K\ge 0 \\ 0 & \text{ if } N>0 \land K=0 \\ \sum\limits_{i=1}^{\min\left(\left\lceil \frac{N}{2} \right\rceil, s_0\right)} f(N-i, K-1, i) & \text{ otherwise} \end{cases} $$ Here we can get the answer to the original problem by calling $f(N, K, N)$ . Python code for the same: import time start_time = time.process_time() def countWays(n, k, prev, v): if n == 0: return [v.copy()] if k == 0: return [] sm = [] for x in range(1, min(prev, (n+1)//2)+1): v.append(x) sm = sm + countWays(n-x, k-1, x, v) v.pop() return sm N = 10 K = 5 a = countWays(N, K, N, []) print(len(a)) for b in a: print(b) print(N, K, time.process_time() - start_time) Next steps I am looking for a closed form formula, or a polynomial (w.r.t. $N$ ) time algo for the above. This might be too close to the partition problem for it to be solved in polynomial time, but I am not sure how to verify that. If this is too diffixult, I will accept special cases of $K=N$ or $K = \lfloor \log_2 N \rfloor +1$ as well.

title: How many steps are needed to turn one "a" into at least 100,000 "a"s using only the three functions of "select all", "copy" and "paste"?
body: Suppose that at the beginning there is a blank document, and a letter "a" is written in it. In the following steps, only the three functions of "select all", "copy" and "paste" can be used. Find the minimum number of steps to reach at least $100,000$ a's (each of the three operations of "select all", "copy" and "paste" is counted as one step). If the target number is not specified, and I want to get the exact amount of "a"s, is there a general formula? This is a fascinating question. My friend and I discussed it for a long time that day, but to no avail. What I started thinking about was – If the steps of "select all", "copy" and "paste" are roughly counted as one step. Each step makes the number $\times2$ , so it is a geometric progression with a common ratio of 2. Let $a_{n}≥100000 \: (n\in \mathbb{N})$ , where $a_{1}=1$ . According to the general formula of geometric progression: $a_{n}=a_{1}\times q^{n-1}$ We can get: $n=17$ So if the three operations of "select all", "copy" and "paste" are each counted as one step, there are a total of $17×3=51$ steps But this ignores a problem: can we paste all the time? So this seems to be an interesting optimization problem, and we need to find a strategy to minimize the number of steps from one "a" to one hundred thousand "a"s. Select all + copy + paste: These three operations double the number of "a"s. If there are currently $n$ "a"s, then there will be $2n$ "a"s after the operation. Paste: This operation will add the number of "a"s equal to the clipboard content. If there are $k$ "a"s in the clipboard, then there will be $(n+k)$ "a"s after the operation. We define a function $f(n)$ that represents the minimum number of steps required to reach $n$ "a"s. Initially, we have one "a", so $f(1) = 0$ . If we choose the doubling operation, $f(2n) = f(n) + 3$ . If we choose the paste operation, then $f(n+k) = f(n) + 1$ , where $k$ is the number of "a"s in the clipboard. Then I started to get confused because I realized that it seemed that every step was facing optimization, and it seemed to be complicated. I started to use function comparison to get $n=14$ as the minimum value, but I realized that it was only optimized once.

title: a question of gamma distribution and negative binomial
body: this is the 9th exercise of chapter 7.4 from fundamentals of probability with stochastic process(4th): a manufacturer produces light bulbs at a poisson rate of 200/hr. the probability that a light bulb is defective is 0.015. during production, the light bulbs are tested and defective ones are put in a special can that holds up to a maximum of 25 light bulbs. on average, how long does it take until the can is filled? one way to solve the problem is using $$\lambda_{defective}=200*0.015$$ and it matches the answer provided by the author. what i want to ask is, i tried another method using combination of negative binomial random variables and gamma distribution but the answer turned out to be wrong. but i couldn't find the problems. $$\sum_{n=25}^\infty {n-1 \choose 25-1}p^{25}q^{n-25}\int_{t=0}^\infty tf(t)dt $$ where p is 0.015(the defective rate) and t represents the gamma random variable with parameter (25, 200) i just skip the details of calculation and the final answer turned out to be $$\frac{25*26}{\lambda*p^2}$$ i don't explain my thinking process very clearly, or the whole question will be too long. if you want further clarification. just let me know. ##calculation process: $$\sum_{n=25}^\infty {n-1 \choose 25-1}p^{25}q^{n-25}\int_{t=0}^\infty tf(t)dt$$ $$= \sum_{n=25}^\infty {n-1 \choose 25-1}p^{25}q^{n-25}\operatorname{E}[T \mid N]$$ $$= \sum_{n=25}^\infty {n-1 \choose 25-1}p^{25}q^{n-25}\frac{n}{\lambda}$$ $$= \frac{1}{\lambda}\sum_{n=25}^\infty \frac{n!}{24!(n-25)!} p^{25}q^{n-25}$$ $$= \frac{25}{\lambda}\sum_{n=25}^\infty {n \choose 25} p^{25}q^{n-25}$$ $$= \frac{25}{\lambda*p}\sum_{n=25}^\infty {n \choose 25} p^{26}q^{n-25}$$ $$= \frac{25}{\lambda*p}\sum_{m=26}^\infty {m-1 \choose 26-1} p^{26}q^{m-26}$$ $$= \frac{25}{\lambda*p}*\frac{26}{p}$$

title: Proving $\frac{\tan A}{1-\cot A}+\frac{\cot A}{1-\tan A}=\sec A\csc A+1$
body: This problem is from S. L. Loney’s 1896 Trigonometry book: Prove: $$\frac{\tan A}{1-\cot A}+\frac{\cot A}{1-\tan A}=\sec A\csc A+1$$ Eventually I was able to prove the identity but I want to know if there is a simpler way to prove it. Here is my proof: $\frac{\tan A}{1-\cot A}+\frac{\cot A}{1-\tan A}=$ $\Large \frac{\frac{\sin A}{\cos A}}{1-\frac{\cos A}{\sin A}}+\frac{\frac{\cos A}{\sin A}}{1-\frac{\sin A}{\cos A}}=$ $\Large \frac{\frac{\sin A}{\cos A}}{\frac{\sin A-\cos A}{\sin A}}+\frac{\frac{\cos A}{\sin A}}{\frac{\cos A-\sin A}{\cos A}}=$ $\frac{\sin A}{\cos A} \cdot \frac{\sin A}{\sin A-\cos A}+\frac{\cos A}{\sin A} \cdot \frac{\cos A}{\cos A-\sin A}=$ $\frac{\sin^2 A}{\cos A(\sin A-\cos A)}+\frac{\cos^2 A}{\sin A(\cos A-\sin A)}=$ $\frac{1-\cos^2 A}{\cos A(\sin A-\cos A)}+\frac{\sin^2 A-1}{\sin A(\sin A-\cos A)}=$ $\frac{\sin^2 A}{\sin A(\sin A-\cos A)} + \frac{-\cos^2 A}{\cos A(\sin A-\cos A)} + \frac{1}{\cos A(\sin A-\cos A)} + \frac{-1}{\sin A(\sin A-\cos A)}=$ $\frac{\sin A}{\sin A-\cos A} + \frac{-\cos A}{\sin A-\cos A} + \frac{\sin A}{\sin A\cos A(\sin A-\cos A)} + \frac{-\cos A}{\sin A\cos A(\sin A-\cos A)}=$ $\frac{\sin A-\cos A}{\sin A-\cos A} + \frac{\sin A-\cos A}{\sin A\cos A(\sin A-\cos A)}=$ $1 + \csc A\sec A=$ $\sec A\csc A + 1$ Q. E. D. Edit: I just realized this is a duplicate of the following question: Trigonometric identity: $\frac {\tan\theta}{1-\cot\theta}+\frac {\cot\theta}{1-\tan\theta} =1+\sec\theta\cdot\csc\theta$

title: Determining the Equality of Two Field Extensions
body: Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $0$ . Let $F(\alpha)/F$ be a finite extension of degree not divisible by $3$ . Is is true that $F(\alpha^3)=F(\alpha)$ ? If we assume that they are not equal, since $\alpha$ is a root of $g(x)=x^3-\alpha^3\in F(\alpha^3)[x]$ , $$[F(\alpha):F(\alpha^3)]\le3$$ If the degree of $F(\alpha)/F(\alpha^3)=3$ , we get a contradiction, as then $3$ divides the degree of $F(\alpha)/F$ . If $F(\alpha)\ne F(\alpha^3)$ , then we conclude that $[F(\alpha):F(\alpha^2)]=2$ , and so $g(x)$ must be reducible in $F(\alpha^3)$ . Specifically, we have that $g(x)$ has a linear factor in $F(\alpha^3)$ . If it is true that $F(\alpha^3)=F(\alpha)$ , we should get a contradiction from this. However, I can find no reason for why this generates a contradiction. Moreover, my argument is not involving the fact that we're in a characteristic $0$ field. On the other hand, I'm failing to find a counter example. Every extension I can think of for which $F(\alpha^3)\subsetneq F(\alpha)$ is such that $3$ divides the order of the extension $F(\alpha)/F$ .

title: Bruhat decomposition of $SL_3$
body: I would like to know the Bruhat decomposition of $SL_3$ . In Chevalley Group Theory, we have the following theorem: Let $G$ be the Chevalley group, and $G=\langle\mathfrak{X}_\alpha | \alpha \;\text{are} roots \rangle$ . Then $$ \bigcup_{w\in W}BwB=G. $$ Where $B$ is generated by $U$ and $H$ , and $U = \mathfrak{X}_P, P=\{\alpha \; \text{are roots}|\alpha > 0\}$ , $H$ is generated by all $h_\alpha(t)$ . $h_\alpha(t)=w_\alpha(t)w_\alpha(1)^{-1}.$ $w_\alpha(t)=x_\alpha(t)x_{-\alpha}(-t^{-1})x_\alpha(t)$ $\mathfrak{X}_\alpha= \{x_\alpha(t)= \exp(tx_\alpha)\}$ For $SL_3$ , its Borel subgroup $B$ is all upper triangular matrices with determinant 1, and the Weyl group is isomorphic to $S_3$ , corresponding to permutation matrices: $\{e, s_1, s_2, s_1s_2, s_2s_1, s_1s_2s_1\}$ . $$ SL_3=\bigcup_{w\in W}BwB. $$ we have the following double coset representatives： $$ \begin{aligned} &1.B\cdot e\cdot B \\ &2.B\cdot s_1\cdot B \\ &3.B\cdot s_2\cdot B \\ &4.B\cdot s_1s_2\cdot B \\ &5.B\cdot s_2s_1\cdot B \\ &6.B\cdot s_1s_2s_1\cdot B \end{aligned} $$ We can calculate them separately, which is not difficult. I'm not sure if the above results are correct, anyway, I hope to understand $SL_3$ from this decomposition. Taking it a step further, I would like to ask what profound implications this decomposition has in the Chevalley group. And what does it have to do with the Reductive Groups . What is the use of this decomposition in the representation of algebraic groups or the representation theory of Lie algebras, and how to analyze it in this example ? Looking forward to your reply, thank you!

title: A diagrammatic proof of antipode being antihomomorphism in a Hopf algebra
body: Let $(H, \mu, \eta, \Delta, \epsilon, S)$ be a Hopf algebra with $S: H \to H$ denoting the antipode. By definition, $S$ is the convolution inverse of $1: H \to H$ in $\operatorname{End}(H)$ , with the convolution product $f*g$ given by the composition $$H \xrightarrow{\Delta} H \otimes H \xrightarrow{f \otimes g} H \otimes H \xrightarrow{\mu} H$$ It is commonly known that $S$ is an antihomomorphism ( $S(xy) = S(y)S(x)$ ), but the only proof I am aware of is via direct computation (like Prop III.3.3 in Kassel's Quantum Groups). While I can spend time on understanding the proof, I wonder if there is a more categorical proof of this. In the end, a Hopf algebra makes sense in any symmetric (or braided) monoidal category, and $S$ being an antihomomorphism simply translates to asking the equality $$S \circ \mu = \mu \circ \tau \circ (S \otimes S): H \otimes H \to H$$ (where $\tau: H \otimes H \to H \otimes H$ is the braiding). Thus, my speculation is that a purely diagrammatic proof should exist, unless the statement is not true for a general symmetric monoidal category (in which case I would like to know what makes vector spaces special). Does anyone have a reference?

body: For given statistical model $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{P})$ , where $\mathcal{P}=\{B(1,\theta)^{\otimes n}:\theta\in (0,1)=\Theta \}$ , $B(1,\theta)$ is a Bernoulli -trial with success probability $\theta$ , we can show that: $$C=\left(\overline{x}_n-\frac{u_{1-\alpha/2}}{\sqrt{n}}\sqrt{\overline{x}_n(1-\overline{x}_n)},\overline{x}_n+\frac{u_{1-\alpha/2}}{\sqrt{n}}\sqrt{\overline{x}_n(1-\overline{x}_n)}\right)$$ $$D=\left(\sin^2(\arcsin(\sqrt{\overline{x}_n})-\frac{u_{1-\alpha/2}}{2\sqrt{n}}),\sin^2(\arcsin(\sqrt{\overline{x}_n})+\frac{u_{1-\alpha/2}}{2\sqrt{n}})\right)$$ are asymptotical confidence intervals for $\theta$ with confidence level $1-\alpha$ , where $\alpha \in (0,1)$ and $u_{\beta}$ is the $\beta$ -quantile of the standard-normal distribution, $\beta \in (0,1)$ . title: Counterexample of Weak Convergence when Function is not Bounded
body: Ex. 10.1.6 Let $M > 0$ , and let $f, f_1, f_2, \cdots :[0, 1] \rightarrow [\frac{1}{M}, M]$ be Borel measurable functions with $\int_0^1 f \; d\lambda = \int_0^1 f_n \; d \lambda = 1$ . Suppose $\lim_n \frac{f_n (x)}{f(x)} = 1$ for each fixed $x \in [0, 1]$ . Define probability measures $\mu, \mu_1,\mu_2, \cdots$ by $\mu (A) = \int_A f\; d \lambda$ and $\mu_n (A) = \int_A f_n \; d \lambda$ , for Borel $A \subseteq [0, 1]$ . Prove that $\mu \Rightarrow \mu$ . Ex. 10.1.7 Give an example to show that the result of the previous exercise is false if the functions $f, f_1, f_2, \cdots$ are strictly positive but are not required to be between $\frac{1}{M}$ and $M$ . I have attempted Ex. 10.1.6, but can't find counterexample for Ex. 10.1.7 , esp. that I am struggling with the condition that $\lim_n \frac{f_n (x)}{f(x)} = 1$ . My attempt on Ex. 10.1.6 For $x \in [0, 1]$ , assume that $A = [0, x)$ . Then $|\mu_n (A)| = |\int_A f_n \; d \lambda| = |\int_0^x f_n \; d \lambda| \leq ( M - \frac{1}{M} )x \leq ( M - \frac{1}{M} )$ . $\therefore \mu_n (A)|$ is bounded. By assumption, $\lim_n \frac{f_n (x)}{f(x)} = 1$ $\therefore \forall \varepsilon > 0: \exists N\in \mathbb{Z}^+: n \geq N\Rightarrow | \dfrac{f_n (x)}{f(x)} - 1| < \varepsilon$ , i.e. $|f_n (x) - f(x)| \leq \varepsilon |f(x)| < \varepsilon M$ . $\therefore f_n (x) \rightarrow f(x)$ . $\therefore$ By bounded conv. thm, $\lim_n \int_0^x f_n \; d \lambda = \int_0^x f \; d \lambda$ . $\therefore \mu_n \Rightarrow \mu$ . Obviously, " $|f_n (x) - f(x)| \leq \varepsilon |f(x)| < \varepsilon M$ " makes that $f_n$ and $f$ being bounded are necessary. Another help for counterexample? Thanks. Source: Rosenthal, J. S. title: Invariance of set distances with $\varepsilon$-neighbourhoods
body: I am trying to prove something involving distances between sets which I believe to be true (at least intuitively), but can't seem to get to the end. The situation is as follows. Let $\Omega$ be a non-empty open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ and let $K \subset \Omega$ be compact. For any set $A \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ and $r > 0$ , define $$A_{\text{ball}}(r) = \bigcup_{a \in A} B(a, r)$$ to be the $r$ -neighbourhood of $A$ . Suppose there is another compact set $K' \subset \Omega$ containing $K$ such that $\text{dist}(K', \partial\Omega) = \text{dist}(K, \partial\Omega)$ and the closure $\overline{K'_\text{ball}(r)}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ for some $r > 0$ is contained in $\Omega$ . Then it follows that $$\text{dist}\left(K'_\text{ball}(r), \partial \Omega\right) = \text{dist}\left(K_\text{ball}(r), \partial\Omega\right). \tag{1}\label{1}$$ Here, $\text{dist}(A, B) = \inf\{|a - b| : a \in A, b \in B\}$ . The reason why I think this is true is because intuitively, what this says is that if I have two sets that are of the same distance away from the boundary of a set that contains them both, then if I uniformly fatten up the first two sets by the same sufficiently small amount, the new distances to the boundary should change by the same amount. What I have tried to prove (after drawing some pictures) is that $\text{dist}\left(K_\text{ball}(r), \partial\Omega\right) = \text{dist}(K, \partial\Omega) - r$ and after playing with the infimums, I've managed to get $\text{dist}\left(K_\text{ball}(r), \partial\Omega\right) \geq \text{dist}(K, \partial\Omega) - r$ . But I can't seem to get the other inequality so that equality is established. I would expect that this reasoning doesn't depend on $K$ so that we would also get $\text{dist}\left(K'_\text{ball}(r), \partial\Omega\right) = \text{dist}(K', \partial\Omega) - r$ , and then everything would follow from my assumptions. So could I get suggestions on how to obtain $\text{dist}\left(K_\text{ball}(r), \partial\Omega\right) \leq \text{dist}(K, \partial\Omega) - r$ , if it is in fact true? Finally, if all of the above holds, would \eqref{1} still be true if I replaced $A_\text{ball}(r)$ with a cube neighbourhood $$A_\text{cube}(r_1, \dots, r_n) = \bigcup_{a \in A} \prod_{i = 1}^n \{x_i \in \mathbb{R} : |x_i - a_i| < r_i\}$$ and kept the analogous assumptions throughout?

title: Distributional equality between SDEs
body: Let $B(t)$ be a Wiener process. title: Is there a characterization of monos and epis in (co)slice and arrow categories?
body: I'm working through Borceux's Categorical Algebra, and I'm curious about problem 1.11.10. It says to characterize the monomorphisms, epimorphisms, and isomorphisms of $C/I$ , $I/C$ , and $\textrm{Arr}(C)$ (slice, coslice, and arrow categories). It's clear that isomorphisms are "just the isomorphisms of $C$ " appropriately restricted (pairs of them in the case of $\textrm{Arr}(C)$ ). Furthermore, epis/monos from $C$ are clearly preserved whenever one (or a pair) can be found in the new category. But it seems like the process of constructing these categories might not be reflective of epis/monos, in the sense that some arrows (or pairs) might become epis/monos due to losing some arrows that could witness their non-epi/mono status in $C$ . Is there a better characterization of monos/epis in (co)slice and arrow categories, or is this about all that can be said in general? Edit : It seems like in the category of sets, the projection $C/I\to C$ preserves monics, but not epics (consider any arrow in $C/I$ with codomain $Id_I: I\to I$ , then any given arrow, $f$ , that can be post-composed with it must be an iso and is necessarily the unique arrow from its domain ( $Id_I$ ) to its inverse ( $f^{-1}$ )). The dual is true for $I/C$ and epics.

title: Proof of existence of $\epsilon$-nets in infinite metric spaces.
body: The following is an excerpt from these lecture notes : Given a metric space $(X, d)$ , a subset $Y$ of $X$ is said to be an $\epsilon$ -net if For $a, b \in Y$ , we have $d(a, b) \geq \epsilon$ . For all $x \in X$ , there exists an $a \in Y$ such that $d(x, a)<\epsilon$ . For every finite metric space $X$ and every $\epsilon>0$ , it is clear that there exists an $\epsilon$ -net. It can easily be found by the following greedy algorithm: Start with a single point in the net $N$ . While there exists a point $x \in X$ such that $\min _{a \in N} d(a,x)>\epsilon$ , add $x$ to $N$ , and repeat. Clearly since $X$ is finite this terminates, and we are left with an $\epsilon$ -net at the end. Using Zorn's lemma one can argue this even for infinite metric spaces, but we will not go into the proof. Question My question is about the last point from the excerpt. Can anyone point me to a reference for a proof on the existence of $\epsilon$ -nets in arbitrary metric spaces? Or at least the idea of how Zorn's lemma is applied?

title: Further questions about correspondence theorem for rings and quotient ring isomorphism.
body: Background This is a continuation of a post about correspondence theorem for rings , I will repost what I have written here from the Background section of that post here for ease of reference: The ideal in a commutative ring $R$ generated by eleements $a_1,\dots, a_n$ is denoted by the wedge bracket notation: $$\langle a_1,\dots, a_n \rangle$$ and sometiems the more informative noatation $$Ra_1+Ra_2\dots +Ra_n.$$ Proposition 4.32 (Euclidean division with polynomials). If $R$ is a commutative ring and $g$ is a non-zero polynomial in $R[X]$ such that its leading coefficient is a unit of $R$ , then for eveyr $f$ in $R[X]$ there exist unique polynomials $q,r$ in $R[X]$ so that $$f=gq+r\quad\text{and}\quad \text{deg }r<\text{deg }g\text{ or }r=0.$$ In particular, if $R$ is a field, then the above holds for all non-zero $g$ . Propositiion 4.49 (Correspondence theorem).: Let $\phi: R\to A$ be a surjective ring homomorphism. (Here $R,A$ need not be commutative.) Let $\mathcal{J}$ be the family of ideals of $R$ containing $\text{ker }\phi$ . and $\mathcal{L}$ the family of ideals of $A$ . (1) If $J \in\mathcal{J}$ , then $\phi(J) \in\mathcal{L}$ (2) If $L \in\mathcal{L}$ , then $\phi^{-1}(L) \in \mathcal{J}$ (3) If $J \in\mathcal{J}$ , then $\phi^{-1}(\phi(J))=J.$ (4) If $ L\in\mathcal{L}$ , then $\phi(\phi^{-1}(L))=L.$ (5) The mapping $\mathcal{J}\to \mathcal{L}$ defined by $J\mapsto \phi(J)$ is a bijection whose inverse is the mapping $\mathcal{L}\to \mathcal{J}$ defined by $L\mapsto \phi^{-1}(L)$ (6) If $J\in \mathcal{J}$ , then $R/J\cong A/\phi(J) $ An Illustration of the Correspondence Theorem The isomorphism in item 6 of the correspondence theorem can be useful in detectin the nature of some quotient rings. Here is a scenerario which could occur. $\quad$ Say $R$ is a commutative ring and $a,b\in R$ . What can Proposition 4.49 reveal about the quotient ring $R/\langle a,b\rangle$ ? Well, the canonical projection $\phi: R\to R/\langle b\rangle$ is a surjective homomorphism, and its kernel is the principal ideal $\langle b\rangle$ . The ideal $\langle a,b \rangle$ contains $\langle b\rangle$ . By a simple verification the image $\phi(\langle a,b \rangle)$ is the ideal $\langle \phi(a),\phi(b)\rangle$ inside $R/\langle b\rangle$ . Since $\phi(b)=0$ the image $\phi(\langle a,b\rangle)$ is the principal ideal $\langle \phi(a)\rangle$ . According to the correspondence theorem $$R/\langle a,b\rangle\cong (R/\langle b\rangle)/\langle a\rangle).$$ The right side is a succession of quotients of two principal ideals, which more readily be deciphered. $\quad$ For example, let us describe the quotient ring $\Bbb{Z}[X]/\langle X^2+1,X-2 \rangle$ . Start with the substitution map $\phi:\Bbb{Z}[X]\to \Bbb{Z}$ given by $f\mapsto f(2).$ This is a surjection and its kernel is the ideal $\langle X-2\rangle$ . Indeed, $\langle X-2\rangle\subset \text{ker }\phi$ because $X-2$ has a root at $2$ . On the other hand $f\in \text{ker }\phi$ . Since $X-2$ is monic, Proposition 4.32 gives a polynomials $q,r$ in $\Bbb{Z}[X]$ such that $f=(X-2)q+r$ and $r$ is constant. From $f(2)=0$ it follows that $r=0,$ and thus $f\in \langle X-2\rangle$ . $\quad$ The correspondence theorem gives a bijection between the ideals of $\Bbb{Z}[X]$ containing $\langle X-2\rangle$ and the ideals of $\Bbb{Z}$ . Now $\langle X^2 +1, X-2\rangle$ contains $\langle X-2\rangle$ . By item 6 of the correspondence theorem $$\Bbb{Z}[X]/\langle X^2 +1, X-2\rangle\cong \Bbb{Z}/\phi(\langle X^2 +1, X-2\rangle).$$ In $\Bbb{Z}$ the ideal $$\phi(\langle X^2 +1, X-2\rangle)=\langle \phi(X^2+1),\phi(X-2)\rangle=\langle 2^2+1,2-2\rangle=\langle 5\rangle$$ Thus $$\Bbb{Z}[X]/\langle X^2 +1, X-2\rangle\cong \Bbb{Z}/\langle 5\rangle=\Bbb{Z}_5.$$ The original quotient is isomorphic to the finite field $\Bbb{Z}_5$ . $\quad$ Let us see what happens if we carry out the process in a different order. Take the substitution map $\psi:\Bbb{Z}[X]\to\Bbb{Z}[i]$ given by $f\mapsto f(i)$ . This is a surjective homomorphism and its kernel is $\langle X^2+1 \rangle$ . Indeed, $\langle X^2+1 \rangle\in \text{ker }\psi$ because $i$ is a root of $X^2+1$ . On the other hand let $f\in \text{ker }\psi$ . Since $X^2+1$ is monic, Euclidean division gives polynomials $q,r$ in $\Bbb{Z}[X]$ such that $f=(X^2+1)q+r$ and $r$ is of the form $a+bX$ for some $a,b$ in $\Bbb{Z}$ . Since $f(2)=0$ we get $r(2)=a+bi=0.$ By the nature of complex numbers $a=b=0$ , and thus $r=0$ . Having seen that $f=(X^2+1)q$ it follows that $\text{ker }\psi=\langle X^2+1 \rangle$ . By item 6 of the correspondence theorem $$\Bbb{Z}[X]/\langle X^2 +1, X-2\rangle\cong \Bbb{Z}[i]/\psi(\langle X^2 +1, X-2\rangle) =\Bbb{Z}[i]/\langle \psi(X^2+1),\psi(X-2)\rangle=\Bbb{Z}[i]/\langle i-2\rangle.$$ Putting all of this together we come up with the less than obvious discovery that $$\Bbb{Z}[i]/\langle i-2\rangle\cong \Bbb{Z}_5.$$ Questions I am stil having trouble with the following: "By a simple verification the image $\phi(\langle a,b \rangle)$ is the ideal $\langle \phi(a),\phi(b)\rangle$ inside $R/\langle b\rangle$ . Since $\phi(b)=0$ the image $\phi(\langle a,b\rangle)$ is the principal ideal $\langle \phi(a)\rangle$ ," and how the author used $R/\langle a,b\rangle\cong (R/\langle b\rangle)/\langle a\rangle).$ to show $\Bbb{Z}[X]/\langle X^2 +1, X-2\rangle\cong \Bbb{Z}/\langle 5\rangle=\Bbb{Z}_5$ ? For the first, I understand that $\phi(\langle a,b \rangle)=\langle \phi(a),\phi(b)\rangle$ , but then to say that "....is the ideal $\langle \phi(a),\phi(b)\rangle$ inside $R/\langle b\rangle$ , does it mean $\langle \phi(a),\phi(b)\rangle\subset R/\langle b\rangle$ ? Also, how does $\phi(b)=0$ imply $\phi(\langle a,b\rangle)=\langle \phi(a)\rangle$ ? As for the second, $\Bbb{Z}[X]/\langle X^2 +1, X-2\rangle\cong \Bbb{Z}/\langle 5\rangle=\Bbb{Z}_5$ , how does their compuation connect to $R/\langle a,b\rangle\cong (R/\langle b\rangle)/\langle a\rangle)$ , in the sense that $\Bbb{Z}[X]/\langle X^2 +1, X-2\rangle\cong (\Bbb{Z}[X]/\langle X-2\rangle)/\langle X^2 +1\rangle)$ Thank you in advance
