title: Can a convex function with a unique support be non-differentiable?
body: Let $\mathrm{M}$ be an open convex set of a normed space and $f:\mathrm{M} \to \mathbf{R}$ a continuous convex function . Definition. A support of $f$ at $v \in \mathrm{M}$ is an affine function $x \mapsto f(v) + L(x-v)$ ( $L$ is a linear form) such that $f(x) \geq f(v) + L(x-v).$ A well-known result asserts that at every $x \in \mathrm{M}$ the function $f$ will have at least one support at $x$ and that if $f$ is differentiable then it has a unique support. I am interested in the reciprocal proposition. Suppose that for some $v \in \mathrm{M},$ the function $f$ has a unique support on $v.$ Does this imply that $f$ is differentiable at $v$ ? Here is a partial result in $\mathbf{R}^d.$ In this case, it is known that a convex function with partial derivatives will be differentiable. Therefore, suffices to show that if $f$ has a unique support at $v$ then $f$ has partial derivatives. To prove this, consider any unit $u \in \mathbf{R}^d,$ the convex function $t \mapsto f(v + tu)$ (defined on an open interval around the origin) also has a unique support; it is well-known that real-line convex function $\varphi$ defined on an open interval will have sided-derivatives everywhere on that open interval, in this case, it is easy to see that any $m \in [\varphi_-'(0), \varphi_+'(0)]$ will make the affine function $t \mapsto \varphi(0) + mt$ a support of $\varphi.$ With the aforementiones property of convex function on intervals, if $t \mapsto f(v+tu)$ has a unique support at $t = 0,$ its sided-derivatives must coincide and this imply that $f$ has directional derivatives at $v$ (in every direction). In particular, $f$ has partial derivatives and therefore $f$ is differentiable. Obviously, this case does not extend to infinite dimensions and I do not know a proof or a counterexample. Addendum: the following theorem can be proved. Theorem: Suppose that $\mathrm{M}$ is open and convex and $f:\mathrm{M} \to \mathbf{R}$ is convex. In order for the directional derivative $\partial_u f(v) = \lim\limits_{h \to 0} \dfrac{f(v+hu)-f(v)}{h}$ to exist (at a given $v \in \mathrm{M}$ ) and every unit vector $u$ it is necessary and sufficient that $f$ should have a unique supporting hyperplane at $v.$ When this is the case, $u \mapsto \partial_u f(v)$ is linear. Sketch of proof. After two translations, $f(0) = 0.$ Suppose now $f$ has unique support at the origin. Then, there exist one and only one linear form $L$ such that $f(x) \geq L(x)$ . For any unit $u,$ we have $f(tu) \geq t L(u)$ for all $t$ small enough. Thus, the convex function $t \mapsto f(tu)$ dominates the linear form $t L(u)$ ; by Banach's extension theorem, the linear form $tL(u) = L(tu)$ (defined on $\mathbf{R} u$ ) extends to a linear form (on $\mathrm{V}$ ) such that $\bar L(x) \leq f(x),$ that is to say, the extension $\bar{L}$ is a supporting hyperplane of $f$ at the origin and it therefore coincides with $L.$ Thus, $t \mapsto f(tu)$ cannot have more than one supporting line at the origin and this implies that this function is differentiable, i.e., $f$ has directional derivative at the origin with direction $u.$ Reciprocally, suppose $f$ has directional derivative. Convexity of $f$ shows it must have at least one supporting hyperplane at the origin, i.e., there is a linear form $L$ such that $f(x) \geq L(x).$ For unit $u$ and all small $t,$ $f(tu) \geq L(tu) = t L(u).$ Dividing by $t$ and considering cases $t > 0$ and $t < 0,$ we see that $\partial_u f(0) = \lim\limits_{t \to 0} \frac{f(tu)}{t} = L(u)$ and therefore $L$ is uniquely determined and $\partial_u f(0)$ is linear in $u$ . QED Therefore, the original question becomes: Suppose $\mathrm{M}$ is an open convex set of a normed space and $f:\mathrm{M} \to \mathbf{R}$ convex and continuous. Assume $f$ possesses directional derivatives everywhere on $\mathrm{M}$ (and on every direction) and that $u \mapsto \partial_u f(v)$ defines a linear function for every $v \in \mathrm{M}$ . Is $f$ (Frechet) differentiable?

title: Finding $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{5}k^{99}\pmod{5}$
body: This problem is from a great book: $$\color{rgb(128,128,255)}{\text{Discovering Higher Mathematics}}\\\color{rgb(255,128,128)}{\text{Four habits of Highly Effective Mathematicians}}\\\text{By }\color{rgb(0,191,0)}{\text{Alan Levine}}$$ Find the remainder when $1^{99}+2^{99}+3^{99}+4^{99}+5^{99}$ is divided by $5$ . My Approach: $1^{\text{any natural number}}\equiv1\pmod{10}$ Finding the units digit of powers of $2$ : $2^1\equiv2\pmod{10}, 2^2\equiv4\pmod{10}, 2^3\equiv8\pmod{10}, 2^4\equiv6\pmod{10}$ This pattern will repeat for higher integer exponents. Now $99\equiv0\pmod{3}$ , so $4^{99}\equiv4^0\equiv1\pmod{10}$ $5^{\text{any natural number}}\equiv5\pmod{10}$ Adding these: $1+8+7+1+5=22\equiv2\pmod{5}$ My final answer is $2$ . $\color{red}{\text{Question 1:}}$ Is my approach correct? $\color{red}{\text{Question 2:}}$ Is there a faster way to solve this problem? title: Are "other" algebraic extensions of $\mathbb{R}$ similar to $\mathbb{C}$?
body: If we define $\mathbb{R}[x] = \{ c_0 + c_1 x + \cdots + c_n x^n : n\in\mathbb{N}, \forall c_k \in \mathbb{R} \}$ as the set of polynomials with coefficients in $\mathbb{R}$ then I'm familiar with the result that $\mathbb{R}[i] = \mathbb{C}$ , where $i$ is a root of the irreducible (over $\mathbb{R}$ ) polynomial $x^2 + 1$ . Obviously all polynomials of degree 3 or higher are reducible, since all odd powers have at least 1 real root, and every even degree can be factored into irreducible quadratics by the fundamental theorem of algebra — like how $$x^4 + 1 = (x^2 + \sqrt{2}x+1)(x^2 - \sqrt{2}x + 1).$$ But what if we try adjoining roots of other irreducible quadratics to $\mathbb{R}$ , different from $i$ ? For example, what if $\alpha$ is a root of the irreducible quadratic $x^2 - x + 1$ , meaning that $\alpha^2 = \alpha - 1$ ? Obviously this number can be expressed as a traditional complex number involving $i$ , but what can we say directly about the set $\mathbb{R}[\alpha]$ ? Is $\mathbb{R}[\alpha]$ isomorphic to $\mathbb{C}$ since both $\alpha$ and $i$ are roots of a degree 2 polynomial?

title: Using contradiction to validate an argument
body: In general, when we want to establish the validity of the argument $(p_1 \land p_2 \land ... p_n ) \rightarrow q$ , we can establish the validity of the logically equivalent argument $(p_1 \land p_2 \land ... p_n \land \lnot q) \rightarrow F_0$ Note that $\rightarrow$ and $\Rightarrow$ mean differently in the notation style of this book: $\rightarrow$ is just ordinary implication while $\Rightarrow$ means tautology. Now, let's use contradiction to establish the validity of this argument: $\lnot p \leftrightarrow q\\ q \rightarrow r\\ \lnot r$ $\therefore$ p I am trying to understand why, in the above exercise ( page 105 here ), the author says that $$[(\lnot p \leftrightarrow q) \land (q \rightarrow r) \land \lnot r \land \lnot p] \Rightarrow F_0.$$ Yeah, when the implication is a tautology then $p$ must be true; but why is $\Rightarrow $ used here?

title: The parabola V(Y-$X^2$) in $(𝔽𝑝) ^2$ could it be not irreducible?
body: The Parabola V(Y- $X^2$ ) is the set of couple (x,y)∈ $(𝔽𝑝) ^2$ such that $y=x^2$ , p is a prime number and 𝔽𝑝 is the finite field with p elements. title: Proof explanation: how to see that $(u_n)$ is bounded above by $v_0$
body: I am new to this and I am trying understand this proof of Monotone-sequences property $⇒$ least upper bound property. Let $A$ be a non-empty set that's bounded above. Pick $u_0, v_0$ such that $u_0$ is not an upper bound for $A$ and $v_0$ is an upper bound. Now do a repeated bisection: having chosen $u_n$ and $v_n$ such that $u_n$ is not an upper bound and $v_n$ is, if $(u_n + v_n)/2$ is an upper bound, then let $u_{n + 1} = u_n$ , $v_{n + 1} = (u_n + v_n)/2$ . Otherwise, let $u_{n + 1} = (u_n + v_n)/2$ , $v_{n + 1} = v_n$ . Then $u_0 \leq u_1 \leq u_2 \leq \cdots$ and $v_0\geq v_1 \geq v_2 \geq \cdots$ . We also have $v_n - u_n = \frac{v_0 - u_0}{2^n} \to 0.$ By the monotone sequences property, $u_n\to s$ (since $(u_n)$ is bounded above by $v_0$ ). Since $v_n - u_n \to 0$ , $v_n \to s$ . We now show that $s = \sup A$ . If $s$ is not an upper bound, then there exists $a\in A$ such that $a > s$ . Since $v_n \to s$ , then there exists $m$ such that $v_m < a$ , contradicting the fact that $v_m$ is an upper bound. To show it is the \emph{least} upper bound, let $t < s$ . Then since $u_n \to s$ , we can find $m$ such that $u_m > t$ . So $t$ is not an upper bound. Therefore $s$ is the least upper bound. I don't understand how they got to the part "By the monotone sequences property, $u_n\to s$ (since $(u_n)$ is bounded above by $v_0$ )". Here's what I thought about: From "Pick $u_0, v_0$ such that $u_0$ is not an upper bound for $A$ and $v_0$ is an upper bound." I figure these two inequalities: $\exists a \in A$ s.t. $a>u_0$ and $a \leq v_0$ $\forall a \in A$ imply $u_0 < v_0$ and consequently? $u_n < v_n$ . Using this fact and from $\frac{v_n-u_n}{2}>0$ I got $u_{n+1} \geq u_n$ and $v_{n+1} \leq v_n$ . Monotone sequence propery states that if a sequence is increasing/decreasing and bounded above/below, it converges to some limit. I just don't know how to connect the dots here? Can someone check if I wrote all inequalities correctly and how to go from here to see that $(u_n)$ is bounded above by $v_0$ ?

title: Countable system of differential equations
body: I'm interested in solving the following countably infinite system of ODEs \begin{equation} \frac{d}{dt}H_{n,k}\left(t\right)=\left(-p\right)nH_{n,k}\left(t\right)+\left(-q\right)nH_{n,k+1}\left(t\right)+pkH_{n+1,k-1}\left(t\right)+qkH_{n+1,k}\left(t\right),\qquad n,k=0,1,2,..., \end{equation} where $p,q>0$ are constants and we set $H_{n,-1}\left(t\right)\equiv 0$ , while the initial conditions are $$H_{n,k}(0)=\begin{cases} 1 & n\geq1,k=0,\\ 0 & \mathrm{otherwise.} \end{cases}\qquad\qquad n,k=0,1,2,...$$ Following a similar (but simpler) problem, see [1], I set out to define the generating function $$G(x,y,t):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}H_{n,k}\left(t\right)x^{n}y^{k},$$ where $x,y \in (-1,1)$ . Observe that: \begin{align*} \frac{\partial G}{\partial t} &= \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{d}{dt}H_{n,k}\left(t\right)x^{n}y^{k}, \\ x\frac{\partial G}{\partial x} &= \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}nH_{n,k}\left(t\right)x^{n}y^{k}, \\ \frac{x}{y}\frac{\partial G}{\partial x} &= \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}nH_{n,k}\left(t\right)x^{n}y^{k-1} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\sum_{k=-1}^{\infty}nH_{n,k+1}\left(t\right)x^{n}y^{k}, \\ \frac{y}{x}\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(yG\right) &= \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\left(k+1\right)H_{n,k}\left(t\right)x^{n-1}y^{k+1} = \sum_{n=-1}^{\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}kH_{n+1,k-1}\left(t\right)x^{n}y^{k}, \\ \frac{y}{x}\frac{\partial G}{\partial y} &= \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}kH_{n,k}\left(t\right)x^{n-1}y^{k} = \sum_{n=-1}^{\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}kH_{n+1,k}\left(t\right)x^{n}y^{k}. \end{align*} Summing the first equation multiplied by $x^{n}y^{k}$ over $n,k=0,1,...$ yields $$\frac{\partial G}{\partial t}=-px\frac{\partial G}{\partial x}-q\frac{x}{y}\frac{\partial G}{\partial x}+p\frac{y}{x}\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(yG\right)+q\frac{y}{x}\frac{\partial G}{\partial y}-R\left(x,y\right),$$ where $$R(x,y)=\left(-q\right)\frac{1}{y}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}nH_{n,0}\left(t\right)x^{n}+p\frac{1}{xy}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}kH_{0,k}\left(t\right)y^{k}+q\frac{1}{x}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}kH_{0,k}\left(t\right)y^{k}.$$ The boundary terms correspond to: \begin{align*} -q\frac{1}{y}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}nH_{n,0}(t)x^{n} & =-q\frac{x}{y}\left.\frac{\partial G}{\partial x}\right|_{y=0},\\ p\frac{1}{xy}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}kH_{0,k}(t)y^{k} & =p\frac{1}{xy}\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(yG)\right|_{x=0},\\ q\frac{1}{x}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}kH_{0,k}(t)y^{k} & =q\frac{1}{x}\left.\frac{\partial G}{\partial y}\right|_{x=0}. \end{align*} Hence the PDE is $$ \frac{\partial G}{\partial t}=-px\frac{\partial G}{\partial x}-q\frac{x}{y}\frac{\partial G}{\partial x}+p\frac{y}{x}\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(yG\right)+q\frac{y}{x}\frac{\partial G}{\partial y}-q\frac{x}{y}\left.\frac{\partial G}{\partial x}\right|_{y=0}+p\frac{1}{xy}\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(yG)\right|_{x=0}+q\frac{1}{x}\left.\frac{\partial G}{\partial y}\right|_{x=0}$$ with the initial condition $$G(x,y,0):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}H_{n,k}\left(0\right)x^{n}y^{k}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}H_{n,0}\left(0\right)x^{n}=\frac{x}{1-x}.$$ Though the the resulting PDE seems complicated (and maybe ill-posed? the boundary terms look suspicious), which suggests that either I have a mistake in my calculations or that this simply is not the right approach (though the approach itself using the generating functions seems elegant in my eyes). I have also considered using a laplace transform but that would yield a countably infinite system of algebraic equations (though linear). But since I have little knowledge about this topic, I have no yet done so. If you believe this would be a better approach, please share your views. [1]: https://math.stackexchange.com/q/4279739/262202

title: Mean Angle to Points on a Cone
body: Consider a cone of radius $r$ and height $h$ . Define $m=\frac{h}{r}$ . Its equation is given below. \begin{align} z(x,y)=-m\sqrt{x^2+y^2}+h\hspace{5mm}z\geqslant0 \end{align} Let $O$ represent the center of the cone's base (the origin). Let $A$ represent the apex of the cone $(0,0,h)$ . Let $P_j$ represent an arbitrary point on the cone. Define $\phi_j$ as $\angle AOP_j$ . What is the mean value of $\phi_j$ assuming a uniform distribution of points across the manifold? I believe the answer may be $\frac{\pi}{2}-\arctan\left(\frac{h}{2r}\right)$ . My approach: Let's define $\bar \phi$ as the average value of $\phi_j$ . It can be calculated as shown below: \begin{align} \bar \phi&=\cfrac{\int\limits_0^{\pi/2}\cfrac{\phi d\phi}{\tan\phi+m}}{\int\limits_0^{\pi/2}\cfrac{d\phi}{\tan\phi+m}} \end{align} We'll break this up into the following two integrals: \begin{align} I_1&=\int\limits_0^{\pi/2}\cfrac{\phi d\phi}{\tan\phi+m} \\ I_2&=\int\limits_0^{\pi/2}\cfrac{d\phi}{\tan\phi+m} \end{align} These are two very challenging integrals. I have solved $I_2$ , as shown below. However, I have not been able to solve $I_1$ . Solution for $I_2$ \begin{align} I_2&=\int\limits_0^{\pi/2}\cfrac{d\phi}{\tan\phi+m} \end{align} First, we'll multiply the integrand by $\frac{\sec^2\phi}{1+\tan^2\phi}$ . \begin{align}I_2&=\int\limits_0^{\pi/2}\cfrac{\sec^2\phi d\phi}{(\tan\phi+m)(1+\tan^2\phi)} \end{align} Next, we'll substitute. \begin{align} u&=\tan\phi \\ du&=\sec^2\phi d\phi \\ [0,\pi/2)&\mapsto[0,\infty) \\ \\ \implies I_2=\int\limits_0^\infty\frac{du}{(u+m)(u^2+1)} \end{align} Now we must do a partial fraction decomposition. \begin{align} \frac{A}{u+m}+\frac{Bu+C}{u^2+1}&=\frac{1}{(u+m)(u^2+1)} \\ A(u^2+1)+(Bu+C)(u+m)&=1 \\ \end{align} Case 1: $u=-m$ \begin{align} A(m^2+1)&=1 \\ A&=\frac{1}{m^2+1} \end{align} Case 2: $u=0$ \begin{align} A+Cm&=1 \\ \frac{1}{m^2+1}+Cm&=1 \\ Cm&=\frac{m^2+1}{m^2+1}-\frac{1}{m^2+1} \\ C&=\frac{m}{m^2+1} \end{align} Case 3: $u=-2m$ \begin{align} A(4m^2+1)+(-2B+C)(-m)&=1 \\ \frac{4m^2+1}{m^2+1}+2Bm^2-\frac{m^2}{m^2+1}&=1 \\ 2Bm^2+\frac{3m^2+1}{m^2+1}&=1 \\ 2Bm^2&=\frac{m^2+1}{m^2+1}-\frac{3m^2+1}{m^2+1} \\ B&=-\frac{1}{m^2+1} \end{align} Let $k=\frac{1}{m^2+1}$ , then rewrite the coefficients. \begin{align} A&=k \\ B&=-k \\ C&=km \end{align} Rewriting $I_2$ accordingly, \begin{align} I_2&=\int\limits_0^\infty\frac{k}{u+m}-\frac{ku-km}{u^2+1} du \\ I_2&=\lim_{n\to\infty}k\ln|u+m|\bigg\rvert_0^n-\frac{k}{2}\int\limits_0^\infty\frac{2u}{u^2+1} du+km\int\limits_0^\infty\frac{du}{u^2+1} \\ I_2&=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left[k\ln|u+m|\bigg\rvert_0^n-\frac{k}{2}\ln|u^2+1|\bigg\rvert_0^n+km\arctan(u)\bigg\rvert_0^n\right] \\ \end{align} To match the coefficients of the first two valuations, note $\ln|x|=\frac{1}{2}\ln x^2$ . \begin{align} I_2&=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left[\frac{k}{2}\left(\ln(u+m)^2-\ln(u^2+1)\right)\bigg\rvert_0^n+\frac{km\pi}{2}\right] \\ I_2&=\frac{k}{2}\lim_{n\to\infty}\left[\ln\left(\frac{u^2+2mu+m^2}{u^2+1}\right)\bigg\rvert_0^n+m\pi\right] \\ I_2&=\frac{k}{2}\left(m\pi-2\ln|m|\right) \end{align} Substituting $k=\frac{1}{m^2+1}$ , \begin{align} I_2&=\frac{m\pi-2\ln|m|}{2(m^2+1)} \end{align} Substituting $m=\frac{h}{r}$ , \begin{align} I_2&=\frac{\frac{\pi h}{r}-2\ln\left|\frac{h}{r}\right|}{\left(\frac{h}{r}\right)^2+1} \\ I_2&=\cfrac{\pi rh+2r^2\ln\left(\frac{h}{r}\right)}{2(r^2+h^2)} \end{align} My Question I believe $I_1$ is only solvable through nonelementary methods--I have tried integrating by parts but the resulting integrand looks daunting. I would like a solution to that integral OR a different approach to solving the problem. Thank you.

title: Function from $ℕ$ to a non-prime finite field, compatible with addition, and invertible for small values
body: Let $n$ be some positive integer and $𝔽_q$ a finite field. I am looking for (sufficient and/or necessary) conditions on $𝔽_q$ for the existence of a map $φ:ℕ→𝔽_q$ that satisfies the following conditions: For any $i$ , $j\in\{1,…,n\}$ , $φ(i+j) = φ(i) + φ(j)$ ; For any $k$ , $ℓ\in\{2, …, 2n\}$ , $φ(k) = φ(ℓ) \implies k = ℓ$ . Intuitively, this means that from a value $φ(i+j)$ , one can recover the sum $i+j$ (but not, of course, the values $i$ and $j$ that are not unique). Partial answers If $q ≥ 2n-1$ is a prime, we can simply take $φ(i) = i\bmod q$ (the image of $i$ in $𝔽_q$ ). If $q < 2n-1$ , there are more elements in $\{2, …, 2n\}$ than in $𝔽_q$ , so $φ$ cannot exist. More precise question: Is it possible to construct $φ$ for some non-prime fields $𝔽_q$ , provided $q$ is large enough?

title: The measure of what sets is uniquely determined by _finite_ additivity (and translation invariance and normalisation)?
body: I am very familiar with measure theory but am currently wondering about how far finitary methods can take you. Two aspects have to be differentiated: the unique determination and the calculation of areas / volumes. Clearly there is no finitary method to calculate the area of the circle (as $\pi$ is transcendental). However, the area of the circle is uniquely determined as soon as one requires translation invariance, finite additivity and the normalization of the area of the unit square (this is the result of the method of Exhaustion which does not require any infinitary methods but proof by contradiction). I know that Dehn's work on Hilbert's third Problem shows that (in dimension 3 and higher) one can not obtain certain polytopes (such as pyramids) by cutting and gluing cubes finitely many times. This surprising fact again gives a strong restriction on how far finitary methods can lead for the calculation of volume. There seems to be some implications for the theory of valuations on convex bodies. I am only vaguely familiar with this theory but would also be very interested in some exposition on the relations to measure theory. The Jordan measure seems to take the idea of the method of exhaustion to its completion. Let $[0,1]^d \in \mathfrak{F} \subset \mathfrak{P}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ be any ring of sets (in particular closed under finite unions) that is also closed under translation. Lets say that $\mathfrak{F}$ is nice if there is exactly one finitely additive and translation invariant set function $\mu$ with $\mu([0,1]^d) = 1$ . Now my question: Is the system of Jordan measurable sets the largest nice system?

title: Proposition 12 Corollary 1, Section 5.6 of Hungerford’s Algebra
body: Lemma 6.11. Let $F$ be an extension field of $E$ , $E$ an extenion field of $K$ and $N$ a normal extension field of $K$ containing $F$ . If $r$ is the cardinal number of distinct $E$ -monomorphisms $F\to N$ and $t$ is the cardinal number of distinct $K$ -monomorphisms $E\to N$ , then $rt$ is the cardinal number of distinct $K$ -monomorphisms $F\to N$ . Proposition 6.12. Let $F$ be a finite dimensional extension field of $K$ and $N$ a normal extension field of $K$ containing $F$ . The number of distinct $K$ -monomorphisms $F\to N$ is precisely $[F : K]_s$ , the separable degree of $F$ over $K$ . If $F$ is an extension field of $E$ and $E$ is an extension field of $K$ , then $[F:E]_s[E:K]_s=[F:K]_s$ and $[F:E]_i[E:K]_i=[F:K]_i$ . Proof: Exercise; use Lemma 6.11 and Proposition 6.12. Did the author forget to mention $F$ is finite dimensional extension of $K$ or this result holds for infinite dimensional extension? If $F$ is arbitrary extension of $K$ , then we might not even have $N$ normal extension of $K$ containing $F$ . Am I right?

title: Finding mistake in contour integral. $f(z)=\frac{\exp{(-1+i)z}}{z \cdot z^{1/2}}$
body: I'm trying to calculate the following real integral: $$I=2\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{e^{-x^2}\sin(x^2)}{x^2}\mathop{\mathrm{d}x} = \int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{e^{-t}\sin{t}}{t^{3/2}}\mathop{\mathrm{d}t}.$$ I tried defining the complex function: $$f(z)=\frac{\exp{(-1+i)z}}{z \cdot z^{1/2}},$$ which should be holomorphic in $\mathbb{C}\setminus \mathbb{R}_0^{-}$ , when working with the main branch cut of the square root (the argument goes from $-\pi$ to $\pi$ ). I have considered the following contour: I call the integral over the real line $C+iS$ . $C$ and $S$ are equal to: $$C = \int_{\varepsilon}^{R}\frac{e^{-t}\cos{t}}{t^{3/2}}\mathop{\mathrm{d}t}$$ $$S = \int_{\varepsilon}^{R}\frac{e^{-t}\sin{t}}{t^{3/2}}\mathop{\mathrm{d}t}$$ The integral in the big circle vanishes as $R \to \infty$ because the real part in the exponential is negative, also, the denominator is of order $R^{3/2}$ while the length of the curve is of order $R$ . The integral over the imaginary line can be solved substituting $z=it, t \in [R,\varepsilon]$ . The value I obtained is $-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1-i)(C-iS)$ . Finally, the integral of the inner circle is solved substituting $z=\varepsilon e^{it}, t \in [\pi/2, 0]$ . I found: $$\int_{\pi/2}^{0}\frac{\exp{((-1+i)\varepsilon e^{it}) }}{e^{it}\cdot e^{it/2}\cdot \varepsilon^{3/2}}i \varepsilon e^{it}\mathop{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}(-2+\sqrt{2}-i\sqrt{2}) + \mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\varepsilon})$$ Now, the function is holomorphic in an open set containing the contour. So the sum of all these integrals should be $0$ . Solving for $S$ and $C$ , I find that $S=0$ , which is wrong. It should be something positive, according to numerical calculators online. But I cannot find the error. I appreciate any help, thank you in advance :) EDIT: I found the mistake. It was at the very last step, when solving the obtained equation: $$-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1-i)(C-iS)+C+iS+\frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}(-2+\sqrt{2}-i\sqrt{2}) + \mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\varepsilon}) = 0.$$ The real and imaginary parts of this equation are actually linearly dependent, so one can only find this relationship between $C$ and $S$ : $$C+(\sqrt{2}+1)S = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\varepsilon}} + \mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\varepsilon}),$$ which I have checked for low values of $\varepsilon$ and seems correct. So $S$ or $I$ can't be obtained using (only) this contour.

title: The spectral sequence associated to an exact couple without chasing elements
body: $\def\Ker{\operatorname{Ker}} \def\Im{\operatorname{Im}}$ I am trying to prove 011T to myself. It is a result involving an exact couple , its derived exact couple , the spectral sequence one obtains via its iterated derived exact couples, and the filtration $$ 0 = B_1 \subset B_2 \subset \ldots \subset B_r \subset \ldots \subset Z_r \subset \ldots \subset Z_2 \subset Z_1 = E_1 $$ that one associates to a spectral sequence $(E_r,d_r)_{r\geq 1}$ (see paragraph before 011O in Section 011M ). If we work in the category $\mathcal{A}=R\textsf{-Mod}$ of modules over a ring $R$ , then I am able to prove via a diagram chase that $B_{r+1}=g(\Ker\alpha^r)$ and $Z_{r+1}=f^{-1}(\Im\alpha^r)$ . Note that in this case it suffices to show the last claim in 011T 's statement for $T=R$ . Thus, via the identification $E_r=Z_r/B_r$ , the map $d_r:E_r\to E_r$ sends a coset $[x]\in E_r$ to $[gy]\in E_r$ , where $y\in A$ is such that $\alpha^ry=fx$ . My question is: how can one do any of this over a general abelian category $\mathcal{A}$ without resorting to Mitchell's embedding theorem?
